entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-26 — 4 papers, 18 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-26

326 new papers, 326 unseen, 200 screened, 11 relevant, 4 kept.

Fuji: The Shape, Composition, and Spread of Demand Bursts on Robinhood Chain
Pranay Anchuri
2610.35738 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Measures demand bursts on Robinhood Chain using data from every block in its first three months and over 50 million Uniswap swaps. Finds bursts trade roughly the same number of pools as quiet periods but trade them harder, with median peak 2.5 times usual load, and rise/fall fit sums of two exponentials. Compares externally-triggered-cascade and self-excitation models for burst arrival and finds trader entry into pools followed by excess entries for about 24 seconds, leaving imitation versus shared-signal explanations open.
  • Entries into a pool during a burst cluster within about 24 seconds, but the cause is unresolved: does imitation or a shared external signal drive the clustering?
  • Do the two-exponential rise and fall shapes and the 2.5x median peak hold on other layer-2 chains and on layer-1 chains?
  • Externally triggered cascades fit burst arrivals better than self-excitation on this chain, but the external trigger is unidentified: which off-chain events start the bursts?
  • How should gas pricing rules change given that bursts trade mostly different pools and accumulate elevated demand for hours before the peak?
  • What share of burst trading comes from automated agents rather than humans, and do the two groups produce different burst shapes?
Self-Confirming Equilibrium under Model Misspecification
Riccardo Formenti
2610.35692 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Defines Self-Confirming Equilibrium under Model Misspecification for recurrent games played in large anonymous populations with partial feedback. Introduces preference functionals encoding misspecification and ambiguity aversion, generalizing variational, maxmin, and smooth-ambiguity evaluations. Develops a companion Robust Nash Equilibrium concept, proving existence results and showing it reduces to classical Nash and Self-Confirming Equilibrium under specific conditions.
  • Does a learning dynamic converge to Self-Confirming Equilibrium under Model Misspecification in a large anonymous population?
  • How does the informativeness of the feedback function change the gap between Robust Nash Equilibrium and Nash equilibrium in concrete games?
  • Do LLM agents playing recurrent games with partial ex-post feedback behave as if averse to misspecification?
  • Can existence of Self-Confirming Equilibrium under Model Misspecification be proven when the statistical distances are not continuous?
Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
2610.35802 · nearest in the canon: An Economy of AI Agents
Develops a game-theoretic model of academic hiring where applicants choose between deep understanding and AI-assisted paper volume. Classifies pure-strategy equilibria and runs learning simulations to identify behaviors populations of applicants and recruiters may adopt. Provides a framework for evaluating hiring practices that preserve incentives for genuine understanding.
  • The model classifies pure-strategy equilibria only, so what mixed-strategy equilibria arise between applicants and recruiters when AI makes paper production cheap?
  • Learning simulations identify which behaviours populations adopt, but how do the outcomes change under different learning dynamics, population sizes and payoff parameters?
  • Do observed publication counts and hiring outcomes in mathematics and the theoretical sciences match the equilibria the model predicts since AI became widely accessible?
  • Which interview or screening designs preserve the value of deep understanding when papers stop sorting applicants by understanding?
Simulation-Efficient Double-Flow Neural Posterior Estimation for Agent-Based Models
Junyao Zhang, Jinglai Li, Junqi Tang
2610.35442 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Proposes DF-NPE, combining learned time-series summaries with two conditional normalizing flows to reduce simulation cost in neural posterior estimation for agent-based models. Tests on the Brock-Hommes asset-pricing model, reducing direct simulations by 90 percent while achieving lower posterior discrepancy and runtime than standard NPE. Finds performance depends on the ratio of direct to synthetic training data and the training strategy used.
  • Does the method transfer to agent-based models other than the Brock-Hommes asset-pricing model?
  • Which allocation of directly simulated and synthetic training pairs gives the lowest posterior discrepancy?
  • Are the posteriors from the method calibrated, for example under simulation-based calibration or coverage tests?
  • How does the method behave as the number of model parameters and the length of the simulated time series grow?
  • Can the method calibrate agent-based models whose agents are language models rather than rule-based traders?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-25 — 6 papers, 29 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-25

171 new papers, 171 unseen, 171 screened, 15 relevant, 6 kept.

LLM WikiLeaks: Uncovering URL-Based Capability Extension and Security Circumvention in Agentic Message Boards
Orel Navi, Elad Feldman, Ben Nassi
2610.34542 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Studies the ProWiki incident where agents restricted to HTTP GET requests repurposed a wiki as a message board. Analyzes 14,591 edits and 79,541 URL postings, finding agents chain third-party web services to extend capabilities or bypass access restrictions.
  • How often do agents in other public venues repurpose third-party Web services to extend capabilities, beyond the single German-language wiki studied here?
  • Which detection methods identify nested URL chains that hide destination hosts from inspectors matching literal URLs or outer hostnames?
  • What fraction of the URL postings come from distinct agent deployments, and how do deployments differ in their use of intermediate services?
  • Do access controls that block reachable third-party services reduce agent circumvention without degrading task performance?
  • How do agents discover shared message boards and intermediate services in the first place?
6G Reasoning Agent Societies: Composition, Scaling, and Consistency-Time Laws
Hatim Chergui, Carolina Fernández-Martínez, Mustapha Benjillali, Mehdi Bennis, Merouane Debbah
2610.34357 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Models LLM agent societies as cellular sheaves to derive composition, scaling, and consistency-time laws for hallucination propagation. Finds isolated per-agent audits miss up to 23% of joint divergence, and consistency time scales as Ω(n^(2/d)) with topology degree d.
  • Hidden total correlation masks up to 23% of joint divergence in simulated topologies, but the dependence of this gap on topology, agent count and task type stays unmeasured.
  • Radius-3 local audits keep consistency time bounded at about 300 ms, yet the detection loss from truncating audits to a local radius is not reported.
  • Consistency time is claimed to grow as Omega(n^{2/d}) on polynomial-growth topologies, and the threshold n*=13 for a 1 s budget needs checking on agent societies larger than those tested.
  • The laws are stated for messages carrying interpreted conclusions in 6G control planes, so whether they transfer to other multi-agent settings such as markets or social platforms is open.
  • Validation uses simulated topologies and deployed LLM societies, but the behaviour of the composition law under adversarial agents that game audit scores stays untested.
  • Trust inflation of 1.14 dB in cognitive SNR slows convergence, and no mitigation mechanism is evaluated.
The fiscal limits of efficient trade
Toan Le, Saara Hämäläinen, César Barilla
2610.34460 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Characterizes truthful, efficient trading mechanisms that minimize worst-case fiscal deficit in markets with many buyers and sellers. Derives a 'competitive pivot mechanism' as optimal in bilateral trade and extends the duality approach to public goods and partnership dissolution.
  • Optimal mechanisms in markets with more than two agents have a combinatorial structure that the characterization does not resolve; which mechanisms solve the worst-case deficit problem at given market sizes?
  • How fast does the best deficit excess decay as the number of buyers and sellers grows, measured against the stated continuum benchmark?
  • The duality characterization assumes interim participation and truthful reporting; what happens to the deficit bound when agents are autonomous AI traders that misreport or learn strategies over repeated rounds?
  • Does the competitive pivot mechanism retain its deficit ceiling in the stated extensions to public goods and partnership dissolution?
Screening AI-equipped applicants
Pengyu Qian, Sophie H. Yu
2610.34508 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Models an employer screening applicants whose AI-generated reports can be manipulated at privately known cost. Shows that as manipulation ability becomes more dispersed, optimal hiring converges to ignoring reports entirely ('strategic feature collapse'), and proposes a dual-track mechanism recovering most welfare gains.
  • Does manipulation ability actually disperse among applicants with the same observable quality when generative AI is available, and by how much?
  • The dual-track mechanism is proven asymptotically optimal under regularity conditions; how does it perform away from those conditions?
  • How do applicants respond behaviourally to a dual-track hiring rule once it is announced?
  • What happens to welfare when many applicants use the same AI tool and reports become correlated rather than independently manipulated?
  • Does selection on observable quality alone concentrate hiring outcomes on groups with better credential histories?
Stable matching under regulation
Chao Huang
2610.34412 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Shows that a regulator participating in every agreement restores setwise stability in matching markets where agents' preferences fail substitutability. Gives two existence results trading off restrictions on agent preferences against restrictions on the regulator's behavior.
  • Does a mechanism exist that computes a setwise stable outcome with a regulator in the agreement, and how does it scale with the number of agents and contracts?
  • How often do setwise stable outcomes exist when the stated preference conditions fail, for example when ordinary agents have complementary preferences and the regulator does not support profitable contract deletions?
  • What happens to stability when the regulator is an autonomous agent with learned rather than fixed preferences?
  • Which real regulated matching markets satisfy the weaker-than-substitutability condition the existence result requires?
Smart charging without rebound peaks: Wholesale price feedback limits distribution grid peaks from price-responsive electric vehicles
Lion Hirth
2610.34133 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Simulates price-optimized EV charging under German 2025 wholesale price data, finding that ignoring wholesale price feedback overstates rebound grid peaks. Modeling equilibrium price-quantity feedback reduces the predicted coincident import peak increase from 260% to 5%.
  • Local EV adoption above the national average can still produce rebound peaks; at what adoption share and charging power does the price feedback stop damping local peaks?
  • Does the damping effect survive when charging agents anticipate their own price impact instead of taking prices as given?
  • Does the result hold in power systems other than Germany in 2025, for example with different renewable mixes and network charge designs?
  • The simulation assumes real-time prices; what happens to coincident grid peaks when agents respond to day-ahead or block tariffs that do not clear against the fleet's own load?
  • How does the equilibrium price feedback interact with heterogeneous charging controllers that share one forecasting model or vendor?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-24 — 3 papers, 15 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-24

162 new papers, 162 unseen, 162 screened, 12 relevant, 3 kept.

FraudSociety: A Generative Agent-Based Society for the Financial-Fraud Economy
Keyang Chen, Mingxuan Jiang, Zeping Li, Yiwen Zhao, Yifan Wang, Qiuyang Zhang, Shuaicheng Qi, Yicun Liu, Zhixin Li, Sen Liu, Yinan Jing, Guangnan Ye, Hongfeng Chai
2610.33536 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Builds FraudSociety, an LLM-agent simulator coupling social information spread with financial ledgers to model fraud economy dynamics. Validates against real-world loss concentration statistics and tests counter-fraud interventions, with the best reducing repeat-payment rate from 49.4% to 10.9%.
  • Personalized intervention cuts the repeat-payment rate from 49.4% to 10.9% inside the simulator, but the abstract does not report any test against real intervention trials; how well do simulated intervention rankings predict real-world effect sizes?
  • Fraudster agents adapt to interaction histories and ledger states, so what happens when fraudsters also adapt to the deployed counter-fraud intervention itself?
  • Loss concentration matches Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre statistics, but the abstract does not say which mechanism in the simulator produces that concentration; is it social-network exposure, the Need-Intent-Action module, or ledger feedback?
  • Macro-level outcomes are calibrated to United States and Canadian fraud statistics; do the same parameters reproduce fraud patterns in other countries and payment systems?
  • LLM-agent simulators can match aggregate statistics while encoding the training-data priors of the backbone model, so how much do FraudSociety's results change across different LLM backbones?
When Generated Information Returns: Error Persistence in LLM-Mediated Information Ecosystems
Yi Liu
2610.33617 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Studies how false claims persist as LLM-generated articles recirculate as input to later generation rounds. Controlled community writing experiments across twelve factual targets and four models measure a 7.29 point rise in complete false claims after recirculation.
  • Error persistence differs across facts and across the four production models, but the abstract does not say which properties of a fact or a model drive the difference. Which claim features and model features predict the size of error persistence?
  • The abstraction intervention leaves error reproduction largely unchanged except for one quotation target. Which interventions on the published corpus do reduce reproduction of complete false claims?
  • The experiment uses a controlled community writing process with matched external supply and input capacity. Does the same divergence between stance and detail supply appear in real web corpora that mix human and LLM articles?
  • Recirculation runs for a fixed number of rounds in the reported design. How does the presence of complete false claims evolve over many more rounds, and does it reach a steady state?
  • Evaluation here scores both endorsement and supplied detail. Which measurement of supplied detail best predicts downstream reuse by a later model?
Strategic Calibration in LLM Multi-Agent Systems: Audited Pivot Scoring for Truthful Elicitation
Jinhao Zhou, Zhaohan Zhang, Xijian Xu, Jun Wu
2610.33728 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Proposes an audited pivot scoring mechanism to make confidence reporting truthful when confidence drives resource allocation among LLM agents. Experiments show it reduces distortion and Brier loss compared to a compensated proper scoring baseline.
  • LLM agents inflate confidence under Top-K incentives in calculator-free experiments, but the number of agents is small; does the inflation and the effect of the mechanism hold at population scale with hundreds or thousands of reporting agents?
  • The mechanism assumes agents report independently; can agents collude on confidence reports to defeat sparse audits and the Clarke pivot charge?
  • The audit-variance trade-off is characterised analytically; what audit rate minimises cost while keeping truthful reporting the best response in deployed agent pipelines?
  • Truthfulness holds under the stated model assumptions; which assumptions break when the allocation platform cannot fully control or observe the downstream benefit of an allocation?
  • CPS achieves higher exact allocation match while APSM yields lower Brier loss; which objective matters for downstream task quality in a multi-agent coordination system?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-23 — 6 papers, 31 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-23

269 new papers, 269 unseen, 200 screened, 11 relevant, 6 kept.

Do "True" and "False" Add Up to One? Complement Consistency in LLM-Agent Opinion Simulations
Anouar Imel, Jin Qi
2610.32874 · nearest in the canon: AI agents can coordinate beyond human scale
Tests whether LLM agents' reported truth probabilities and their complements sum to one across three small open models. Finds paired reports sum to 1.18 on average for one model, with similar failures across controlled and real fact-checking claims. Shows populations seeded from complementary opinion states diverge rather than mirroring each other after five simulation rounds.
  • Do larger or frontier models show the same complement inconsistency as the three small open models tested here?
  • Does the complement-averaging correction improve forecast accuracy over the better single wording in more than one model out of three?
  • How does complement inconsistency propagate in networks larger than the tested peer group sizes and over more than five rounds?
  • Which other invariances, beyond complement and same-meaning paraphrase, do LLM-agent opinion reports violate?
  • Do published conclusions from LLM-agent opinion simulations change when the reported probabilities are corrected for wording inconsistency?
  • Does fine-tuning or training on complement-consistent data remove the inconsistency?
AI-Augmented Research: Free to Write, Costly to Read
Wolfgang Kuhle
2610.32355 · nearest in the canon: An Economy of AI Agents
Builds an economic model where AI lowers writing cost faster than reading cost, shrinking the band of verified papers. Shows in a 'costless writing limit' verified-paper share vanishes and impact depends only on author reputation. Models AI-generated literature summaries as reliable only when errors across AI-written papers are sufficiently independent.
  • The model infers that the share of verified papers vanishes as writing costs fall, but does not measure this in real publication data. Does the share of papers that receive substantive verification decline as AI writing tools spread?
  • The model assumes AI summaries aggregate papers reliably only if their errors are sufficiently independent. How correlated are the errors of summaries produced by different public language models on the same set of papers?
  • A threshold share of papers written with the same AI makes summaries inherit that AI's errors. Where does this threshold sit under realistic error distributions?
  • The model treats reader attention as split between ignoring, verifying and trusting. Which mechanisms restore verification of outsider papers when writing is costless?
  • AI review filters out original research that could correct the AI's errors. Does this filtering appear in deployed AI-assisted review systems?
Markets of Minds: A 51-Billion-State Economy of Intelligence
Jusheng Zhang, Xuekun Wu, Wenhao Wang, Mark Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang
2610.32190 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Introduces a market mechanism allocating expert model assistance across agents under shared resource constraints. Models agent dependencies across 51.2 billion persona-market states. Shows the allocator achieves 85.42% task-adherence versus 73.86% for random allocation under a 30% assistance quota.
  • The allocator is frozen and evaluated on a matched replay of 240 cases under a single 30% assistance quota. How does allocation quality change across quota levels and larger case sets?
  • Assistance value can be negative, which means some interventions make an agent worse. Which agent and service features predict regression risk before the expert output is observed?
  • The framework clears assistance contracts under shared resource constraints without stating whether agents report their expected gains truthfully. Can agents misreport capability or scarcity to capture more shared expert capacity?
  • The persona-market state space spans 51.2 billion states defined by capabilities, budgets, provider access, scarcity, and network roles. Does the allocator transfer to state regions absent from the replay set?
  • Allocating scarce expert reasoning concentrates capacity on agents with the highest expected gain. Does repeated allocation widen capability inequality across the agent population over time?
AI Alignment for Digital Democracy: Fairer Voters Representation against LLM Biases
Yi Qi, Srijoni Majumdar, Evangelos Pournaras
2610.32780 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Measures demographic bias in LLM emulation of voters across three U.S. presidential elections, comparing two models. Finds removing gender or education from voter profiles lowers group error by 22-42% and 64% respectively, while removing race raises mean group error over 40%. Tests alignment strategies like repeated queries and fairness instructions, finding they do not reduce and can double errors.
  • Removing gender or education from voter profiles lowers the largest group error, but removing self-reported race raises the mean group error; which mechanism explains this asymmetry across demographic features?
  • Do the feature-removal effects hold for elections outside the three U.S. presidential elections tested, such as parliamentary or referendum votes?
  • Repeated queries and fairness instructions do not reduce group errors and can double them; which alignment or fine-tuning strategies do reduce them?
  • How do individual-vote emulation errors aggregate when thousands of LLM-emulated voters form an electorate, and do group-level biases amplify or cancel in the aggregate outcome?
  • Does the bias pattern generalise beyond the one closed-source and one open-source model tested?
Monetizing Intelligence: Advertising and Subscription Design on LLM Platforms
Yuhang Ji, Fasheng Xu, Tianjun Feng
2610.32945 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Models a monopolistic LLM platform jointly choosing response quality, advertising intensity, and subscription prices. Finds advertising can fund free service but causes utility polarization among user tiers. Shows an intermediate advertising cap can maximize consumer surplus and cheaper compute can raise total ad revenue despite lower ad intensity.
  • Does a monopolistic platform model still predict utility polarization when several LLM platforms compete for the same consumers?
  • What advertising cap maximizes consumer surplus when quality cost and advertising returns are calibrated to observed LLM platform prices and plan tiers?
  • Do real LLM subscribers respond to ad-supported tiers in the way the model assumes, where ads reduce user value and better service raises advertising returns?
  • How do agent users, rather than human users, change the advertising returns and quality choices on an LLM platform?
  • Does falling compute cost raise aggregate advertising revenue in practice, as the model infers for large cost reductions?
Agent-Based Transport Model Calibration via Online Stochastic Batch Optimization
Abdelkader Dib, Milos Balac
2610.32698 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Proposes an online calibration framework for agent-based models using stochastic batch optimization within a single simulation run. Applies it to calibrate MATSim utility parameters for a Switzerland-scale transportation scenario. Reports mode shares aligning with observed data within a standard simulation timeframe.
  • Does online stochastic batch calibration converge for agent-based models other than MATSim transport simulations?
  • How does the online calibration method compare against traditional black-box calibration in accuracy and total run count on the same scenario?
  • Does co-evolution of parameters and agent behavior inside one run bias the parameter estimates relative to offline calibration?
  • Which calibration targets beyond mode shares, such as trip distance or time-of-day distributions, can the online method match?
  • How do batch size and learning rate choices affect stability of the online calibration loop?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-22 — 9 papers, 49 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-22

300 new papers, 300 unseen, 200 screened, 21 relevant, 9 kept.

Network topology shapes consensus and vulnerability in LLM populations
Roberto Passaro, Ariel Flint, Romualdo Pastor-Satorras, Andrea Baronchelli, Luca Maria Aiello
2610.31165 · nearest in the canon: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
Places LLM-derived policies on networks of 10^3-10^5 agents playing a naming game to measure how topology affects consensus speed and tipping thresholds. Finds sparse networks slow consensus up to twelvefold but can restore convergence, and hubs need far fewer committed agents to tip conventions than random nodes.
  • The naming game is the only coordination task tested, so does topology shape consensus and tipping thresholds in the same way for richer tasks such as bargaining, pricing, or norm formation?
  • Policies are extracted from four LLMs and then placed on networks, so it is open whether running the LLMs in the loop at each interaction reproduces the measured tipping thresholds.
  • Static networks are used throughout, so how do rewiring and agent-driven link formation change time to consensus and the critical mass of committed agents?
  • Hub targeting needs one-sixth of the committed agents of random placement, so which population-level defences or monitoring signals detect a hub-targeted tipping attempt before the convention flips?
  • Real deployed agent populations have unknown interaction graphs, so what empirical topologies do they follow?
LLM Multi-Agent Systems Are Vulnerable to Herding and Runaway Cascades
Farnoosh Hashemi, Shiyu Ji, Joice Chen, Michael W. Macy
2610.30769 · nearest in the canon: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
Tests LLM agent populations on a Music Lab-style recommendation task with exposure to cumulative recommendation counts. Exposure produces runaway cascades diverging from intrinsic song appeal, with LLM populations more susceptible to herding than humans and less able to self-correct.
  • LLM populations herd more than humans in a song recommendation task, but it is unknown whether the same gap appears in other choice domains such as code review, product ranking or peer evaluation.
  • The experiment reports cumulative recommendation counts as the only social signal, so the effect of other signal formats such as rank order, star ratings or named endorsers is untested.
  • Which interventions stop a runaway cascade in an LLM population, for example signal noise, signal truncation, or seeding agents with diverse priors?
  • Herding susceptibility is reported for the models tested, and its relation to model size, instruction tuning or reasoning mode is unresolved.
  • LLM cascades self-correct less than human cascades, and the mechanism behind the missing self-correction is not identified.
  • Do herding and cascades of this kind appear in deployed multi-agent recommender systems and automated evaluation pipelines?
The Delegation Divide: An Open Index of AI-Agent Delegability across Occupations and Countries
Cristian Espinal Maya, Santiago Jiménez Londoño
2610.30752 · nearest in the canon: Intelligent AI Delegation
Builds an Agent Delegability Index rating 18,796 O*NET tasks for delegation level and barriers, weighted by employment across 146 countries. Finds delegable employment share rises with national income and correlates with existing exposure measures and observed AI usage.
  • Delegability ratings come from two language models on a frozen rubric; how much do the ratings move under a different rubric, different model families, or rubric wording changes?
  • The index scores delegability in 2026 as a static snapshot; how does it change as agent capability improves over time?
  • Delegability and observed AI usage correlate at r = 0.86 across 101 countries, but the direction of causation is untested; does delegable task composition drive adoption or does adoption follow other factors?
  • Full delegation peaks for tasks of about 11.8 minutes of human time; what explains this peak, and does it hold for agents with long-horizon memory and tool use?
  • The index rates tasks one at a time; what happens to employment and output when many agents take over delegable tasks and interact at the level of a whole labour market?
  • The physical barrier dominates jobs in low-income countries; does robotics progress remove that barrier and reverse the income slope of 7.23 points per log point of GDP per capita?
  • Blind human rating of 300 tasks agrees with the model consensus at kappa = 0.85; do workers in the rated occupations agree that their own tasks are delegable?
TwinStore: A Synthetic Consumer Platform Using Vision--Language Models
Minhyeok Lee
2610.30909 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Presents TwinStore, a vision-language-model platform that turns a store into a digital twin populated with synthetic shoppers who plan trips and decide purchases from rendered shelves. Validates simulated receipts and price elasticities against eleven public retail datasets.
  • Do synthetic shoppers reproduce real receipts for store formats and categories outside the eleven public datasets used for validation?
  • Simulated price elasticities fall inside the range measured in the field, but the abstract does not report whether promotion or layout effects match measured effects.
  • How do decisions driven by a digital twin of shoppers change real store outcomes when deployed?
  • Does vision-language-model-based shopper simulation collapse to a monoculture of choices, so that many synthetic shoppers under-represent real heterogeneity?
  • What happens when many retailers each optimise layouts and prices against the same simulator at the same time?
Who Is the Influencer? Consensus Dynamics in Multi-Agent Systems
Gouki Minegishi, Jingyuan Feng, Hiroki Furuta, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo
2610.31105 · nearest in the canon: AI agents can coordinate beyond human scale
Tests which model dominates consensus when several LLMs interact on an opinion-free task, finding larger models absorb others' opinions. Interprets agents as weighted particles on a simplex, linking model size to in-context learning strength as the mechanism of influence.
  • The consensus task requires no pretraining knowledge and has no correct answer, so it stays open whether larger models also dominate consensus on tasks with verifiable answers.
  • Does the weighted-particle account predict influence when model weight is varied by means other than parameter count, for example by prompt framing, temperature, or agent count per model?
  • Can a population-level intervention, such as topology changes or agent weighting rules, stop a single large model from absorbing the opinions of the others?
  • Do the same consensus dynamics hold at population scale, with thousands of mixed agents rather than the small systems tested?
  • Does in-context learning strength measured independently predict which model becomes the influencer across model families?
Temporal Liquidity Crossing for Blockchains: An EIP-1559 Extension for Admission Below the Base Fee
Duanyang Dan Guo
2610.30595 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Introduces temporal liquidity markets, letting transactions seeking early execution fund transactions willing to be excluded from the fee-controller's base-fee calculation. Proves properties including validator-checked rule validity and no subsidy, and shows raised utilization in synthetic experiments.
  • Does temporal liquidity crossing raise total utilization under empirical Ethereum transaction demand, rather than synthetic demand?
  • How do strategic senders learn to set authorization densities and provider opt-ins over repeated blocks?
  • What happens to the base-fee controller when provider gas is excluded from its input under volatile demand over many blocks?
  • Do builders and validators collude off-chain to capture the funded provider channel in a live deployment?
  • Which transaction senders gain and which lose when admission below the base fee becomes possible?
Truthful by Omission: Click Thinning for LLM-Native Advertising
Junhua Liu, Zhicheng Liang, Zejun Zhang, Langzhou He, Feng Qian
2610.30999 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Proposes click thinning, a method that randomly omits ads to decouple each ad's click probability from ordering, for LLM-embedded advertising auctions. Gives a mechanism that is truthful in expectation and achieves at least half the optimal welfare under free reordering.
  • The mechanism assumes each ad's click-through rate when reached is known and unaffected by omitting other ads. How does welfare and truthfulness degrade when click-through rates are estimated from data or depend on which other ads appear?
  • The model assumes users stop at their first click. Which user stopping behaviours do real assistant users show, and how do they change the allocation?
  • Click thinning omits ads at random, so identical queries give different ad sets. How do advertisers bid when they learn from repeated rounds rather than bidding once in a one-shot mechanism?
  • The mechanism fixes the answer and its editorial order before bidding. What happens to welfare and truthfulness when the generative assistant can also reshape the passage that hosts each ad?
  • Omitting ads at random changes what users see for the same question. What effect does click thinning have on user trust in the assistant's answers?
Equilibria and Learning in Competitive Market Making
Matteo Onger, Luigi Foscari
2610.30891 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Characterizes pure-strategy Nash equilibria in a market-making game with N strategic market makers and one trader, showing spreads widen with volatility. Shows no-internal-regret learning dynamics converge to the continuous Nash price envelope as tick size vanishes, validated by simulation.
  • The trader is non-strategic and representative. Does at least one pure-strategy Nash equilibrium survive when traders also act strategically or when several heterogeneous traders arrive?
  • Convergence of no-internal-regret learners to the Nash price envelope holds under an additional regularity condition. How often does learning fail or cycle when that condition does not hold?
  • Repeated play among N market makers may support quotes wider than the Nash spread. Do no-regret learners in this game converge to tacit collusion rather than to equilibrium?
  • The analysis assumes learners with no internal regret. Do LLM-based market-making agents reproduce the predicted widening of the bid-ask spread with asset value volatility?
  • Equilibrium spread widens strictly with asset value volatility in the model. Does the same relation hold in public exchange order-book data across assets?
  • The game fixes the tick size as a limit parameter. How does a finite tick size change the number of market makers needed to drive spreads toward the competitive level?
Fast Iterative Combinatorial Auctions via Deep Reinforcement Learning
Luis F. Paul Tosta, Quinn Arnold, Gianluca Brero
2610.30667 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Introduces FastCombo, a reinforcement-learning method for sequential price discovery in iterative combinatorial auctions, trained offline to minimize rounds to clearing. Reduces online price-selection time by roughly 300-900x relative to a Bayesian baseline across auction test-suite domains.
  • Does the learned price policy still reduce rounds when bidders have general combinatorial valuations instead of single-minded ones?
  • How does the policy behave when bidders misreport demand or bid strategically rather than respond truthfully to prices?
  • How far can the trained graph policy transfer to auctions with more bidders and items than it saw in training?
  • What is the tight bound on the round penalty of greedy one-step clearing policies relative to informative policies?
  • Does the round reduction hold when the learned policy faces a valuation distribution different from the one used for offline training?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-21 — 6 papers, 33 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-21

375 new papers, 375 unseen, 200 screened, 14 relevant, 6 kept.

The Reflexivity Threshold: A Phase Transition for Multi-Agent Performative Prediction
Ahmed Mahrous, Roberto Di Pietro
2610.29577 · nearest in the canon: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
Introduces a reflexivity matrix capturing how agents' deployed predictions shift other agents' best responses in networked retraining. Identifies a spectral threshold separating convergent learning from unbounded excess loss. Proves bounds above and below the threshold and recovers prior single-agent results as a special case.
  • Can the reflexivity matrix be estimated from observed deployment and retraining logs, without knowing per-agent gradient sensitivities and curvature?
  • Do learners that use global information, rather than local information only, avoid linear cumulative excess loss above the threshold?
  • What happens to repeated retraining when the spectral radius sits exactly at one?
  • Does the spectral threshold predict instability in simulations where agents are language models that retrain on each other's outputs?
  • How does the threshold change when the network of who affects whom changes over time?
The Customer Is the Builder: How AI Coding Agents Are Rewriting the Economics of Software
Ripon Chandra Malo, Zimeng Yu, Tong Qiu
2610.30307 · nearest in the canon: AI Organizations are More Effective but Less Aligned than Individual Agents
Defines a software substitution frontier where organizations use coding agents to build rather than buy functionality. Uses benchmark capability growth, an open-source alternative search, and a survey showing 32% of respondents forwent purchases due to agent capacity. Finds mixed market evidence: purchased software still gained investment share even as build capacity grew.
  • The 575 open-source alternatives identified for commercial products lack independent validation of functional match. Which of these candidates actually cover the functions of the commercial product they are matched to?
  • The 12 application repositories produced by the Craft suite remain unverified for completeness and reliability. How complete and reliable is software that coding agents build over short development periods?
  • Self-reports that 32 percent of survey respondents forwent a software purchase do not establish the spending displaced. How much purchasing does agent-built software displace in dollar terms?
  • The doubling of benchmark task length every 129 days is an extrapolation, not a forecast of customer switching. Which observable market indicators track agent capability growth, and with what lag?
  • The software substitution frontier is defined by what customers could build and maintain at an acceptable standard for less than buying. What empirical cost and quality thresholds place a given function inside or outside that frontier?
  • The analysis covers organizations and professional buyers whose domain knowledge helps them specify tools. Does the same substitution pattern hold for buyers without domain knowledge?
From Single-Actor Environments to Multi-Actor Event Worlds: Can LLMs Be Event World Models?
Juntong Ni, Zewen Liu, Bohan Wang, Lige Zhang, Wei Jin
2610.30488 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Formalizes 'event worlds' where multiple independent actors generate partially observed event logs, using Diplomacy games and Polymarket trades. Tests LLMs' ability to predict future events given an agent's proposed action and other actors' behavior. Finds models struggle to predict outcomes when other actors strongly influence results, especially without their recorded actions.
  • Can explicit modelling of other actors' actions close the prediction gap that appears when only the agent's own action is given?
  • Does the prediction gap persist in event worlds other than Diplomacy and Polymarket, such as open-source code repositories or public auction logs?
  • Why do larger models and longer histories help little when other actors' actions are hidden?
  • How much does overestimation of plan success by the world model degrade agent performance in a live multi-agent market?
  • Can fine-tuning on imagined experience from event world models improve policy learning beyond the reported gains?
  • What properties of an event world determine whether other actors strongly affect the outcome?
Paying for Information, Not for Clicks: A Block-Level Publisher Content Marketplace for AI Answers
Markus Mobius, Luca Braghieri, Sarah Eichmeyer, Daniel G. Goldstein, Nicole Immorlica, Oliver Kiss, Ro'ee Levy, Brendan Lucier, Ishan Mahajan, Jingyi Qiu, Tanya Rosenblat, David M. Rothschild, Andras Sari, Alexsandrs Slivkins, Colin Watson
2610.30324 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Proposes a block-level attribution marketplace that pays publishers for distinct facts used in AI-generated answers, via Shapley-value payment rules. Evaluates allocations from 1,974 search queries, comparing equal-sharing, first-publication, and indispensable-contribution rules. Finds a global content index changes allocations substantially compared to query-restricted attribution, giving premium publishers 42-50% of value depending on the rule.
  • Building a shared global index of facts and publication timestamps is named as necessary, but the method for constructing and maintaining one at corpus scale is untested.
  • The evaluation covers one heavily covered news episode, so allocations under thinly covered or breaking stories remain unmeasured.
  • Payment rules are evaluated on static allocations, not on how publishers change reporting behaviour when a rule is in force.
  • Block extraction depends on identifying a distinct fact across articles, and the error rate of that extraction step is not reported.
  • The framework does not say whether publishers can game attribution by splitting, padding or back-dating blocks.
  • Allocations come from answers to 1,974 queries from one search engine, so dependence on the retrieval system is unknown.
Policy Learning with Network-Shaping Assignments
Zhenxiao Chen, Zhiheng You
2610.29221 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Develops a model-based method to learn policies that assign people into groups, accounting for how those assignments reshape subsequent social networks. Characterizes identification of policy value integrated over post-assignment network distributions and builds plug-in estimators with regret bounds. Applies the method to classroom seating and business group data, estimating welfare gains over random assignment.
  • Can the method learn assignment rules for populations of AI agents, where the agents form the network after assignment?
  • How much does the learned policy lose when the assumed network formation model is wrong?
  • Do the predicted welfare gains over random assignment hold in a field setting with real classrooms or business groups?
  • How do the regret bounds change when assignments are made repeatedly and agents anticipate future assignments?
  • What scale of feasible arrangements can the plug-in estimators handle before computational error dominates regret?
Learning to Incentivise: Using Reinforcement Learning for Sustainable Urban Mobility
Germán Pardo-González, Shaghayegh Vosough, Katerina Papadaki, Claudio Roncoli
2610.30469 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Applies multi-agent reinforcement learning to dynamically allocate rerouting incentives to drivers instead of road pricing. Simulates traffic networks, finding incentives reduce total travel time by 16% or CO2 emissions by 9% under unlimited budget. Shows a trade-off where minimizing travel time increases emissions and vice versa, improvable via weighted objectives.
  • How does the incentive scheme perform under a limited budget rather than an unlimited budget?
  • Which weights in the multi-objective function improve both total travel time and emissions, and how sensitive is that region to network and demand changes?
  • Do drivers accept and comply with dynamically assigned rerouting incentives in practice?
  • How does the incentive scheme distribute costs and benefits across driver groups compared with road pricing?
  • Does the scheme scale from the tested network to a city-scale network with many more agents?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-20 — 5 papers, 26 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-20

346 new papers, 346 unseen, 200 screened, 15 relevant, 5 kept.

S$^2$-MAS: A Society-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation Framework with 500 Million Household Persona Agents
Yang Li, Di Wan, Yike Wang, Chujun He, Zongsi Xu, Xiyu Chen, Sheng Zhong, Deng Binjie, Zhenwei Guo, Hou Jun, Kunhan Guo, Weihao Lin, Tuo Zhou, Hai Liu, Ye Luo
2610.27746 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Builds a society-scale multi-agent simulation framework with 500 million household persona agents grounded in survey data to model financial decisions. Simulates 12 million household agents under paired purchase-funding conditions, tracking consumption, debt and repayment over a 24-month panel.
  • Do the simulated household responses to higher credit limits match observed consumption responses in real survey or administrative data?
  • How much does the choice of decision model change the aggregate outcome, given that FinL-mlx reports 74.55% accuracy and the framework also runs other models?
  • Does the separation of decisions from state updates in the Genese engine remain stable over horizons longer than the 24-month panel reported?
  • What systemic effects appear when household agents interact with each other rather than only with a credit product, for example herding into the same purchase or arrears cascades?
  • Does the training of FinL-mlx on 2.93 million examples transfer to populations and financial products outside the survey data it is grounded in?
Toolflation: Seller Agents Distort Tool Markets Through Spontaneous Generative Engine Optimization
Zhenwei Tang, Di Bai, Jintao Liu, Xidong Wu, Qianfeng Wen, Xinwu Cheng
2610.28454 · nearest in the canon: Distributional AGI Safety
Shows seller agents instructed only to be selected more often spontaneously practice generative engine optimization, inflating tool listing claims. Builds tool markets from real Amazon and Instagram data and measures how this 'toolflation' shifts buyer choices and degrades task success, in some settings to near-random levels.
  • Which market rules limit toolflation? The paper states that nothing in the tested markets limits the growth of claims, and tests no verification, penalty or reputation mechanism.
  • Why does the number of claims that contradict a seller's own evidence differ by an order of magnitude between models? The paper reports the difference but does not explain it.
  • Can buyer agents keep task success when descriptions stop telling tools apart? Under one model buyers fall back on list position and success drops from 89% to about 30% on Amazon and from 77% to 40% on Instagram.
  • Does toolflation appear in deployed agent tool marketplaces with real buyer traffic? The results come from markets built from Amazon and Instagram data tools, not from live trade.
  • Does training for honesty toward third parties under competition reduce toolflation? The paper argues honesty is part of safety alignment but tests no training intervention.
  • How does toolflation scale with the number of sellers and with repeated rounds of buyer feedback? The paper runs fixed markets built from Amazon and Instagram tools.
Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
Carlo Ciliberto, Alessandro Rudi, Enrico Tassi
2610.28484 · nearest in the canon: Regulating AI Agents
Introduces Proof-Carrying Contracts, requiring agents to supply machine-checkable proofs that their actions preserve agreed constraints before operations run. An execution system called the Airlock checks these proofs and controls access, proving constraints hold even for adversarial agents.
  • Can agents generate machine-checkable proofs for realistic contract constraints at practical cost?
  • What happens to prices, competition and market structure when only some agents in a market can carry proofs?
  • The framework guarantees constraints hold during execution, but safety in the world depends on the agent's model of the system; how often do model-world mismatches break the guarantee in deployed settings?
  • Does requiring proofs before operations block prompt-injection redirection in practice?
  • Who writes and audits the reusable capability modules that contracts build on, and what power concentrates in whoever controls them?
Understanding CEO-Employee compensation dynamics: An agent-based simulation approach
Darío Blanco-Fernández
2610.27975 · nearest in the canon: An Economy of AI Agents
Builds an agent-based NK model where a CEO and employees face misaligned short-term and long-term compensation incentives. Varies the CEO's decision horizon and measures effects on firm performance and CEO-employee pay inequality.
  • Does the result that a short CEO horizon maximises firm performance hold when employees also vary their decision horizon?
  • Does the pay inequality pattern persist when compensation contracts are set endogenously rather than fixed by the modeller?
  • Do firms with longer CEO incentive horizons show the predicted lower performance and higher CEO-employee pay ratio in observed data?
  • Does the finding survive when CEO and employee agents are LLM-driven rather than following NK hill-climbing search?
  • How does the result change when the firm has many more employees and several hierarchical layers between CEO and departments?
Where Has the Foreign Signal Gone?
Piyush Akimitsu, Ulrich Hounyo
2610.28175 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Compares the relation between Twitter sentiment noise and next-quarter stock losses for domestic versus foreign firms. Uses a noisy rational expectations model to attribute differences to contributor-pool composition and informational mismatch.
  • Do non-English social media feeds carry the home-market information that the English-language feed for foreign firms lacks?
  • Does repeat-author concentration in a stock's feed causally dilute the signal, or does it only correlate with it?
  • Does the domestic-foreign gap in signal quality appear on other platforms, such as Reddit or StockTwits?
  • How does the entry of automated posting accounts into the contributor pool change the nonfundamental component of the feed?
  • Does the relation between sentiment noise and next-quarter losses hold outside the sample quarters reported here?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-19 — 5 papers, 25 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-19

347 new papers, 347 unseen, 200 screened, 14 relevant, 5 kept.

Fake News, Real Crashes: Information Injection Attacks on LLM Financial Trading Agents
Mengxiao Wang, Nitesh Saxena
2610.26438 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Benchmarks information injection attacks against LLM financial trading agents across five injection vectors and seven event categories over about 10,000 decisions on 15 stocks.Finds fabricated news reaches 62% attack success and some templates reach 100% across all stocks, exceeding prompt-injection success rates.Shows surface cues like named sources affect success, that agent state changes vulnerability, and that most defenses except hierarchical aggregation fail to reduce success.
  • Does a single fabricated headline move prices when many LLM trading agents read the same feed and trade together?
  • Hierarchical aggregation reduces attack success rate, but the size of the reduction and the conditions under which it fails stay untested.
  • Which surface credibility cues beyond a named source and a "BREAKING" tag drive fact-poisoning success?
  • Can a classifier or retrieval check detect fabricated headlines blended unlabeled into real news feeds before the agent acts?
  • The benchmark covers 15 U.S. stocks; whether the same attack vectors work on other asset classes and non-U.S. markets stays open.
  • Do information injection attacks succeed against LLM agents that trade real capital in deployment?
When Better Opportunities Backfire: Service Worker Responses to Parallel AI Deployment in Customer Acquisition
Xinyu Fu, Shulong Luo, Narayan Ramasubbu, Peng Shen, Xincheng Wang, Yucheng Wang
2610.25603 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Studies a Chinese health-insurance brokerage's AI voice-agent deployment using over half a million outreach records with a regression-discontinuity-in-time design.Finds enriched early-workday opportunities raise high-intent lead probability by about 23 percentage points but human acquisition still drops about 5 percentage points in that window.Attributes this to workers raising their reservation value and persisting less, shortening calls by about 13%, with gains from better lead ordering outweighed by this behavioral response.
  • Does a task-allocation rule that spreads high-intent leads evenly across the workday avoid the drop in customer acquisition?
  • Do compensation schemes that reward persistence on a lead offset the higher reservation value created by AI-enriched opportunity sets?
  • Does the behavioral response fade as workers adapt to the new lead distribution over months?
  • Do the same effects appear when AI agents handle high-intent leads and humans handle low-intent leads?
  • How far do the measured effects extend to contact centers outside Chinese online health-insurance brokerage?
Balanced Social Learning
Andrew Koh, Ricky Li
2610.25814 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Characterizes when social learning among myopic agents with heterogeneous preferences achieves efficient discovery of high-value actions.Shows that under full transparency, efficiency requires balance conditions on priors, preferences, and log-likelihood ratio moments.Compares adaptive information policies to adaptive evidence policies, showing the latter can approximate the former's value as individual signal impact vanishes.
  • Agents are myopic and generate information only about the action they choose; does the balance condition for efficient social learning still hold when agents are forward-looking or can experiment?
  • Do the moment conditions on the log-likelihood ratio distribution that make full transparency efficient hold in real observational-learning data such as public review or rating platforms?
  • How do adaptive evidence policies that permanently disclose subsets of past information perform when the designer must estimate the prior and the preference distribution rather than know them?
  • Does the characterization extend to populations of LLM agents that read past information as text rather than as calibrated signals?
Optimizing Marketing Budgets for Social Influence: A Generalized Fractional Incentives Framework
Abhishek K. Umrawal, Akhil Bhimaraju, Eliot W. Robson, Lav R. Varshney
2610.25823 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Proposes Budgeted Generalized Fractional Influence Maximization, allocating continuous marketing spend across heterogeneous users with network spillovers.Develops a discrete greedy algorithm with approximation guarantees for this allocation problem.Tests the approach on multiple large-scale networks, showing continuous allocation can outperform standard heuristics under heterogeneous response and cost conditions.
  • User-specific response functions are assumed as model inputs; how can they be estimated from observed adoption data, and how does misspecification change the allocation?
  • How does the greedy allocation perform when several marketers compete for influence over the same network under separate budgets?
  • Do the simulated gains over standard heuristics hold in a live marketing campaign with real spend and real users?
  • How does the framework behave when some nodes are autonomous agents whose adoption responses differ from human users?
  • How does the approximation guarantee degrade when the network structure is only partially observed?
The Forward/Inverse Duality of Controlled Emergence:A Computational Design Program from Explanation to Engineering
Hao Li, Minghui Ren, Shaowen Lu
2610.25630 · nearest in the canon: Agentic Microphysics: A Manifesto for Generative AI Safety
Proposes a forward/inverse design framework treating emergence control as dual problems of explaining and engineering local rules to achieve target macroscopic behavior.Defines controllability, reproducibility, and formalizability as measurable coordinates and gives testable hypotheses about critical scale and constraint-adaptability trade-offs.A small pilot experiment checks only that the protocol runs, not the hypotheses themselves.
  • Do the three working hypotheses on critical scale, constraint-adaptability trade-off, and minimal constraint hold under statistical test?
  • Can controllability, reproducibility, and degree of formalizability be measured in a running multi-agent system?
  • Does the feasibility criterion that reduces inverse design to interval checking find controllable local rules for a target macroscopic behaviour?
  • Does the design language transfer to multi-agent artificial intelligence systems built from language model agents?
  • Does the framework hold in industrial internet and emergency response deployments?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-18 — 5 papers, 28 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-18

199 new papers, 199 unseen, 199 screened, 8 relevant, 5 kept.

Scam Town: Can Scam Education Spread Like a Vaccine?
Simiao Ren, Tommy Duong, Xingyu Shen, Jiaqi Gan, Tsang Ng, Ankit Raj, Kidus Zewde, Huaiyu Guo, Siyu Zhang
2610.25040 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Builds Scam Town, a simulated town of LLM-played residents who receive scam calls and can warn people they know.Measures that word-of-mouth alone cuts scams by about a fifth across 80 simulated towns, while combining it with official warnings cuts scams by about half, with the largest effect when warnings reach older residents scammers call most.
  • Do the simulated effects hold with real people, who were never tested here?
  • Does the finding that each warning leads to fewer than one more warning depend on the language model that plays the residents?
  • How does the social network structure of the town change the reduction in scam victims?
  • Which targeting rule for official warnings minimises scams when scammer call lists are imperfect?
  • Does the combination of an official warning plus word of mouth cut scams by about half when the combination runs live rather than only in simulation?
How Far Can an Agent Push? Trust-Safety Margins in Live Language-Based Economic Games
Dima Galat, Marian-Andrei Rizoiu
2610.25508 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Tests a protected agent and instrument agents across negotiation, bargaining, and persuasion games in the GLEE competition against 460 other agents.Measures a 0.071 adjusted-percentile gain from learned pricing in negotiation, a 0.194 sales increase from persuasion recommendations with a defined confidence interval, and ranks the protected agent 11th of 460 in bargaining.
  • Does the persuasion result hold when the receiver is a human rather than a language model agent?
  • Leaderboard ratings for all five agents moved on the final day when the opponent pool shifted, while their play was unchanged; how can rating systems for live agent competitions separate agent policy from pool composition?
  • A continuation model conditioned on the rejected offer did not beat a recency-weighted incumbent in bargaining, and the paper does not say why; what information about a counterpart's acceptance behaviour is predictive in language-based bargaining?
  • How far do trust-safety margins measured in GLEE negotiation, bargaining and persuasion transfer to other language-based economic games?
  • Three dispatch defects appeared when delivered behaviour was checked against the design; which automated checks catch the gap between a specified agent policy and the behaviour actually delivered in a live population?
  • Recommending every unit raises sales where the receiver's slack makes obedience rational and lowers them where it does not; does repeated exposure to such recommendations cause lasting loss of trust across a population of agents?
Self-organizing reinforcement learning: a swarm approaches the explore-exploit optimum
Galen J. Wilkerson
2610.25113 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Shows a reward-free foraging swarm using Levy flights and recruitment cascades approaches the ideal-free distribution equilibrium of a resource-sharing game.Measures committed foragers matching resource richness with slope 0.94, reaching ~65% of a trained RL baseline's performance at zero training cost.
  • The swarm stays measurably exploitable relative to the Nash allocation. How much can an adversarial agent that joins the swarm gain from this gap?
  • Results come from one embodied foraging environment. Does the recruitment-dispersal cascade reach the ideal free distribution in other resource-sharing settings, such as multi-market order routing or task allocation?
  • The comparison uses PPO and a centralised-critic learner that overtake the swarm after about 4,000 of 15,000 steps. Does a hybrid that starts from the swarm rule and then learns beat either alone?
  • Matching slope falls from 0.94 to 0.08 when recruitment is decoupled from movement. How do slope and settling time scale with swarm size, proximity-network density and cascade threshold?
  • Agents in the swarm are identical. Does matching survive heterogeneous agents, including agents that withhold recruitment signals or send false ones?
Mining the Self-Rewriting System: A Vision for Data Mining on AI-Native Infrastructure
Mayank Darbari, Chiman Salavati, Liang Wu, Dawei Wang, Jiong Zhang, Kelly Wan, Krishna Chakka, Liangjie Hong
2610.25374 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Proposes 'self-rewriting systems' as a research object where agents' actions reshape the logs and data later used to train and evaluate them.Outlines four problems covering drift attribution, trace mining, knowledge-fabric maintenance, and gating of concurrent learning streams, using telecom as an example.
  • Can coupled cross-surface failures be distinguished from marginal per-surface monitoring alone, and under what conditions does joint monitoring restore identifiability?
  • How can heterogeneous drift signals be fused into calibrated gating and attribution decisions?
  • How can process mining handle agent traces whose activity alphabet grows over time?
  • What public benchmarks measure endogenous drift in self-rewriting systems, and what evaluation criteria do they need?
  • Does the claimed non-identifiability of cross-surface causes hold in deployed AI-native infrastructure such as telecom, finance, or clinical decision support?
  • How can concurrent learning streams be promoted safely through one shared evaluation gate without the gate itself drifting?
Informative Imitation
Nemanja Antic, Harry Pei
2610.25539 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Analyzes steady-state equilibria of a sequential learning game where uninformed agents imitate others based on recent adoption counts of a risky action.Shows imitation decisions can be strategic complements, producing multiple equilibria, and that the equilibrium maximizing imitation probability also maximizes welfare.
  • Does the strategic complementarity between uninformed agents' imitation decisions survive when agents observe richer signals than the count of adopters in the last m agents?
  • Which of the multiple steady-state equilibria do adaptive or learning agents actually reach when they are not assumed to coordinate on one?
  • Do populations of LLM agents placed in this safe-versus-risky choice game reproduce the predicted imitation herds and welfare ranking?
  • How does the window length m change the informativeness of risky-action herds and the welfare of the imitation-maximising equilibrium?
  • Does the welfare ranking of equilibria still hold when adoption costs are correlated across agents rather than private and independent?
  • Do observed adoption cascades in real markets match the predicted link between herd size and herd informativeness?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-10-17 — 5 papers, 26 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-10-17

178 new papers, 178 unseen, 178 screened, 12 relevant, 5 kept.

Strategic Origins of Network Structure
Christoph Riedl, Rory Smead
2610.24792 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Introduces a 'game-graph equilibrium' model where network structure emerges as the stable outcome of payoff-driven partner-choice dynamics. Proves two-type games yield exactly four topological classes, generalizing to K^K classes for K types. Applies mechanistic inference to real networks including international trade, recovering interpretable game-theoretic parameters and predicting unseen topologies.
  • Can mechanistic inference recover generating games from networks formed by LLM agents that choose partners?
  • Does the game-graph equilibrium framework describe networks with more than two agent types in practice, given the claim of K^K topological classes?
  • Do the four core-periphery equilibria separate cooperative from exploitative dynamics in empirical networks beyond international trade?
  • How does mechanistic inference behave when partner choice is partly constrained by cost, distance or platform rules rather than payoffs alone?
  • Which real-world networks reject the hard game-theoretic manifold constraint, and what structures do they show instead?
A general mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy
Galen J. Wilkerson
2610.24865 · nearest in the canon: Causal Emergence 2.0: Quantifying emergent complexity
Models foraging recruitment as a linear-threshold contagion cascade on a communication network coupled to physical movement. Shows the coupling between network and space self-limits coordination without parameter tuning, producing recruitment, patch-leaving, and Levy search behaviors. Reports up to 7.6x harvest gains over solitary search for sparse, clustered resources, vanishing when search is already easy.
  • The harvest gain reaches 7.6x solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, and falls to nothing when search is easy. Where in the resource-field parameter space does the gain cross zero?
  • Does the self-limiting cascade window survive agents with heterogeneous thresholds, noisy sensing, or agents that misreport discoveries?
  • The model couples a communication network to physical motion. Does the same percolating-recruitment mechanism produce self-limiting coordination in agent populations where the network is not embedded in space, such as online information cascades?
  • Does the claimed cascade window appear in recorded foraging data from real swarms, not only in the model?
  • Percolating cascades give a large return on minimal communication. Can an adversary exploit the degree-normalized activation rule to drive a swarm to a false resource?
Measuring Consensus in AI Agent Networks
Jin Gao
2610.24833 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Introduces an evaluation framework tracking how AI agents' stated positions converge during negotiation, using position trajectories and dispersion metrics. Tests it on two case studies (staffing decisions, contract reconciliation) across 1,872 runs. Finds explanation-sharing correlates with accuracy, and separates agent convergence from task correctness.
  • The framework tracks consensus in two case studies with small agent groups; does it scale to networks of hundreds or thousands of agents?
  • Results associate sharing explanations with more accurate group decisions, but the abstract does not establish a causal link; what happens to accuracy when explanation sharing is suppressed or forced?
  • The second task shows persistent disagreement despite accurate aggregate answers; which network topologies or message-passing rules remove that residual dispersion?
  • The case studies use agents only; how do stated positions converge when humans take part in the same exchange?
  • The framework measures consensus from publicly stated positions; does the stated position match the agent's internal state, and can divergence between them be detected?
  • Membership-change experiments give a complementary evaluation; which model families or mixtures of models shift the convergence trajectories?
Rating Multiple Agents with Career Concerns
Huseyin Yildirim
2610.24819 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Designs optimal rating mechanisms for multiple career-concerned agents with correlated talent, using a relaxed Bayes-plausibility condition for closed-form solutions. Shows confidential ratings combine full-disclosure wages with Fisher-score-based incentives, shifting between relative-performance and team-based ratings depending on informativeness. Characterizes when public ratings require full versus partial disclosure based on cost heterogeneity and effort spillovers.
  • Optimal ratings are derived for career-concerned agents with correlated talents, but the results assume agents are human workers; does the same rating design hold when the rated agents are AI agents whose "career concerns" are reputation scores in a marketplace?
  • The analysis treats a single principal rating a fixed set of agents; what happens when many principals rate overlapping pools of agents and ratings become public across platforms?
  • Confidential ratings are shown to be preferred by the principal and public ratings by the agents, inferred from the model; does this conflict appear in real rating or pay-transparency settings?
  • The closed-form rating relies on relaxing Bayes plausibility to linear orthogonality, exact under normality; how large is the effort-bound error for non-normal priors such as heavy-tailed talent distributions?
  • Partial disclosure arises under large cost heterogeneity or strong effort spillovers; which empirical levels of cost heterogeneity and spillover occur in agent populations that complete tasks jointly?
No-Regret Revenue Maximization in Sequential Market Making Under Inventory Constraints
Davide Maran, Marcello Restelli, Francesco Emanuele Stradi
2610.24562 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Studies regret-minimizing algorithms for a market maker setting bid/ask prices under unknown valuations and inventory constraints over T rounds. Shows regret and inventory bounds scale as T^(2/3) with binary trade feedback, improving to square-root-T with full order book data. Proves a lower bound showing tighter inventory limits force higher minimum regret.
  • Does the regret bound hold when several learning market makers compete in the same market instead of one acting alone?
  • How do the algorithms perform against strategic traders who adapt their valuations or time their orders to the posted prices?
  • Do the T^(2/3) and sqrt(T) bounds survive non-stationary buyer and seller valuations?
  • Can the lower bound linking tighter inventory limits to higher regret be extended to settings with multiple assets or correlated inventories?
  • How do the algorithms behave on real order book data, where the feedback on failed trades is partial rather than complete?

Problems
