But How Would AI Agents Run a Town's Economy?
Sajal Regmi, Siddhartha Pudasaini, Chetan Phakami Pun
2609.11108 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Runs a 100-agent LLM-based closed economy simulation for up to 26 weeks. Measures monetary transmission, wage stickiness, and wealth concentration decay after shocks and cash transfers. Finds most money stays static; wealth correlation across weeks drops from 0.964 at 2 weeks to 0.752 at 26 weeks.
  • Agents reprice only 0.3% of 3,981 menu items after a 12x demand shock, and the paper does not say why. Which prompt, tool or incentive change makes LLM agents adjust prices?
  • Wealth rank correlation falls from 0.964 at 2 weeks to 0.752 at 26 weeks, and the paper stops at 26 weeks. Does the distribution keep unfreezing at longer horizons, or does it settle?
  • Swapping the backing LLM moves every measured outcome (p=0.0039), while deleting agent memory moves none detectably. Which model properties drive the economic outcomes?
  • A purely social tool fails 94-97% of the time across two model families. What causes the failures, and do agents ever learn to avoid the tool?
  • Marginal propensity to consume after a cash transfer is 3-4%, indistinguishable from zero. Does the same near-zero propensity appear when human participants trade inside the same economy?
The Oligarch Barely Steers Model Collapse in Multi-Model Ecosystems
Yangze Liu, Zhongyi Han
2609.11146 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Tests recursive training collapse in ecosystems of 3-13 open LLMs mixed by market share, including an injected 90%-share oligarch model. Finds market concentration barely changes collapse speed or destination within the tested range. Shows collapse speed depends instead on which specific models supply the shared training pool, with a susceptibility index explaining speed variation (R^2=0.68).
  • Model collapse tests use 13 open models of 1-4B parameters over five generations; whether the same invariance to market concentration holds for larger models or more generations is untested.
  • The share-weighted susceptibility index explains 68% of speed variance across nineteen arms, leaving the rest unexplained; what other model properties predict how fast an ecosystem drifts?
  • Replacing half the pool with human text roughly halves drift without changing its course; the minimum fraction and the type of human text that slows collapse are not reported.
  • Collapse is measured on a single ruler that registers only a faint trace of the topic shifts caused by share and identity knobs; which metrics detect steering that this ruler misses?
  • The pool mixes outputs by market share and retrains every model from clean base weights each generation; how do collapse speed and destination change under continual fine-tuning or non-uniform pooling rules?
  • Real generative AI markets are an oligopoly, but the experiment injects a probe to force a 90% top share; how do actual market shares and real web text contamination rates map onto the tested range?
A Fragility Spectrum for Recursive Language-Model Training
Yangze Liu, Zhongyi Han
2609.11149 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Runs 13 checkpoints through five generations of shared recursive training and finds a five-fold spread in output diversity loss. Shows collapse susceptibility is a stable per-checkpoint property, not explained by parameter scale or static indicators. Finds cutting top-p sampling at generation time nearly stops collapse across the tested checkpoints.
  • No static indicator tested predicts a checkpoint's fragility under recursive training, so what checkpoint properties do predict it?
  • Fragility is measured with unique 4-gram counts after five generations, so it is open whether the same ordering of checkpoints holds under semantic or task-performance measures of collapse.
  • The experiment fixes one recursive contamination protocol, so it is open whether the checkpoint ordering survives other protocols, such as longer generation chains or asymmetric contamination shares.
  • Tightening top-p nearly stops collapse within three generations for six checkpoints, so how does this intervention trade off against output quality and diversity in the uncontaminated case?
  • The ecosystem has 13 checkpoints sharing one corpus, so it is open how mixed ecosystems behave when fragile and robust models contribute unequal shares of the shared pool.
  • Parameter scale does not explain fragility within a three-size ladder, so it is open whether pretraining data composition or post-training method drives it.
Characterizing Bluesky Content Moderation Service: From Automation of Service to Landscape of Harms
Pushpdeep Singh, Sayeh Jarollahi, Ayan Majumdar, Vabuk Pahari, Abhijnan Chakraborty, Krishna P. Gummadi, Ingmar Weber, Abhisek Dash
2609.11373 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Audits Bluesky's default moderation service using 10.6 million 2025 moderation labels. Measures automation versus human review speed, and finds high precision (0.837) but low recall (0.222) via manual annotation. Clusters frequently labeled posts to characterize the types of harm detected.
  • Bluesky's moderation service reaches precision 0.837 but recall 0.222 on a random sample; which classes of harmful content does it miss most often?
  • How much of the harmful content that the moderation service misses comes from automated or bot accounts rather than human accounts?
  • Does the split between seconds-latency automatic labels and hours-to-days human labels change user posting behaviour after a label is applied?
  • Do the precision and recall figures measured on Bluesky transfer to other decentralized platforms and to labelers other than the default service?
  • Which moderation design achieves higher recall without losing precision when automated labelers and human reviewers are combined in different proportions?
  • How do agreement rates between annotators vary across the nuanced, high-stakes label categories that the audit found need human oversight?
terms.txt: A Consent and Compensation Protocol for Agentic Web Access
Rajarshi Chowdhury
2609.11152 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Specifies terms.txt, a per-path machine-readable access-terms file plus a signed exchange protocol for AI crawlers and agents. Defines what the protocol can enforce, audit, or leave to contract, including HTTP 402 payment negotiation. Reports the implementation adds 0.20-0.65 ms overhead per request on one vCPU.
  • Adoption of terms.txt by sites and crawlers is unmeasured, so what fraction of the top web domains would publish machine-access terms and what terms would they set?
  • Compliance is untested, so how often do named AI crawlers respect declared per-purpose terms compared to robots.txt directives?
  • Pricing under HTTP 402 negotiation is left to contract, so what price levels and market structure emerge when many agents bid for per-path access?
  • The latency figure comes from one vCPU, so how does the exchange scale under concurrent agent traffic at production request rates?
  • The protocol concentrates access control in origins and delegation-token issuers, so does it shift bargaining power toward large AI platforms or toward publishers?
  • Circumvention is cited as a robots.txt weakness, so which evasion strategies defeat Web Bot Auth signatures and signed intent in practice?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-09 — 9 papers, 45 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-09

267 new papers, 267 unseen, 244 screened, 15 relevant, 9 kept.

Cyber-Financial Contagion: Modeling the Propagation of an AI Vendor Compromise Through the Banking System
Alex Leytes
2609.10350 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Builds a four-layer network coupling AI vendors, banks, interbank exposures and customer accounts, with a stochastic epidemic-and-clearing propagation model called CFC-Prop. Runs it on a synthetic dataset of 60 vendors, 220 banks, and thousands of edges, reproducing heavy-tailed loss distributions. Trains an early-warning GNN reaching AUROC 0.82 to flag high-cascade-risk vendors.
  • CFC-Prop runs only on a synthetic network of 60 vendors, 220 banks, about 2,500 vendor-bank service edges and 1,400 interbank exposures, so it is open whether its loss distributions hold on real vendor-bank dependency structures.
  • Which network features drive the heavy-tailed loss distribution in a vendor-compromise cascade model?
  • Patch latency drives cascade size in the model, so which supervisory interventions on patch latency and vendor diversification reduce expected losses most?
  • CFC-GNN reaches AUROC 0.82 using vendor-side incident telemetry, but it is untested whether comparable warning comes from graph structure alone without telemetry.
  • How does contagion change when banks and vendors adapt after an incident instead of holding fixed linkages?
  • Does real vendor incident telemetry support early warning of cascade risk at the accuracy the synthetic experiment reports?
How neighbourhood ideology shapes misinformation belief in densely tied social networks
Soroush Karimi, Marcos Oliveira, Diogo Pacheco
2609.10277 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Builds an agent-based model where misinformation belief depends on individual ideological intensity, claim alignment, and social influence from neighbours. Finds that neighbours' ideological intensity effect on belief depends on how densely those neighbours are connected to one another.
  • Does the model reproduce belief patterns in observed social network data, and with which parameter values?
  • How does the effect of neighbours' ideological intensity change across network topologies other than densely tied ones?
  • Which interventions, such as rewiring or targeted correction, reduce misinformation belief in this model?
  • Do belief dynamics change when agents are language models with ideological personas rather than parametric rule-followers?
  • Do real people update belief in the way the model assumes, given ideological intensity and claim alignment?
Tapes Together Strong: The Co-evolution of Computation and Cooperation
Kunal Jha, Francesco Cicala, Blaise Agüera y Arcas, Blake Aaron Richards, Natasha Jaques, Max Kleiman-Weiner, Eyvind Niklasson
2609.10817 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Introduces Autopoietic Game Theory, coupling social interaction, replication and computation cost in randomly initialized Z80 machine-code programs. Shows cooperative, self-replicating strategies emerge when resource scarcity makes defection self-limiting. Extends the framework to include exogenous reward pressures tied to computation budgets.
  • Does the suppression of stealing hold in substrates other than Z80 machine code?
  • How does spatial assortment change the level of stealing compared with well-mixed populations, measured across a range of resource scarcity levels?
  • Do cooperative strategies that evolve under energy-coupled computation transfer to populations of LLM-based agents that also face compute budgets?
  • Which exogenous task pressures beyond math tasks tied to computation budgets preserve cooperation as a dominant strategy?
  • How large must the population be before parasitic stealing stops being self-limiting?
Where Should Society Draw the Line? A Social Choice Approach to Collective Consent
Chris Dong, Sonja Kraiczy, Rohit Vasishta, Markus Brill, Wesley H. Holliday, Niclas Boehmer
2609.10759 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Develops an axiomatic theory of collective consent, defining sufficient-support, minority-protection and dominance principles. Introduces solution concepts including an Approval-Weighted Veto Core. Tests these concepts on five datasets of political, ethical and moral decisions.
  • How costly is it to compute the Approval-Weighted Veto Core as the number of options and individuals grows?
  • Do the solution concepts resist strategic misreporting of attitudes by individuals?
  • What consent decisions result when the attitudes come from LLM agents rather than humans?
  • Can collective consent concepts serve as runtime guardrails that decide which actions a deployed autonomous system may take?
  • How do the solution concepts behave when a population contains correlated or near-identical attitude profiles, as with agents sharing one base model?
Monitoring Hierarchies in Knowledge Production
Shota Ichihashi, Fei Li, Dihan Zou
2609.10499 · nearest in the canon: Intelligent AI Delegation
Models a principal designing robust contracts for peer monitoring among agents performing related tasks. Finds the optimal contract creates a hierarchy of monitoring authority based on how easily agents can be monitored directly. Shows task diversity improves information value but weakens peer monitoring, distorting task assignment.
  • Does the predicted monitoring hierarchy appear when the agents are LLM agents rather than rationalizable players?
  • How does the tension between task diversity and peer monitoring change when agents can collude on their peer reports?
  • Does confidential random task assignment raise output in real knowledge-producing organisations?
  • Do the robustness results survive when the number of agents grows large and monitoring information becomes noisy?
The Attention Cost of Stable Matching
Victor H. Aguiar, Dian Hong
2609.09693 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Derives rates at which unmatched shares fall under stability versus maximum matching as market size grows, given limited attention. Proposes limited-attention deferred acceptance to preserve valid authorizations and reengage eligible pairs. Applies the model to speed-dating and Chilean school-choice data, finding 9,502 applicants accepting improved placements.
  • The unmatched-share rates of $e^{-\sqrt d}$ and $e^{-d}$ come from an independent random market, so how do they change when preferences are correlated or when agents share a common ranking?
  • LA-DA assumes exact next-best information and persistent execution rights, so how much of its advantage survives when next-best estimates are noisy?
  • What happens to attention-limited stable matching when one side is served by autonomous agents that can screen many more partners per unit time than people can?
  • The Chilean school choice result reports 9,502 applicants accepting higher-ranked or new placements through retained rankings, but how much of that gain transfers to other centralised assignment systems?
  • The speed dating application compares stable and maximum matching on restricted graphs from bilateral reports, so does the same decomposition of missed opportunities and stability loss hold in online matching platforms with one-sided attention logs?
ALIGN-HOLD: Experience Alignment for Real-Time Hold Control in Large-Scale Ride-Hailing Matching at DiDi
Zuhao Zhang, Xu Liu, Kai Wan, Zihao Lu, Li Ma, Shuai Li
2609.09685 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Presents ALIGN-HOLD, a reward-model-based framework learning hold policies for ride-hailing driver-order matching from implicit marketplace preferences. Deploys it on DiDi's platform in a 28-day A/B test covering roughly 100,000 daily passenger requests. Reports improved trip completion, driver income and reduced cancellations versus the production policy.
  • Learning hold policies from implicit marketplace preferences improves trip completion and driver income in one market; does the same reward model transfer across cities with different supply-demand regimes?
  • How does a preference-learned hold policy redistribute income and waiting time across individual drivers and passengers, rather than in platform-level averages?
  • Can drivers or passengers change their behaviour to exploit a hold policy trained on their own past trajectories, and what feedback loop does that create?
  • Filtering low-identifiability interactions removes feedback that cannot be attributed to matching quality; what bias does this filtering introduce into the learned reward model?
  • How closely does simulator-based policy learning for hold control match deployed outcomes, and which simulator assumptions drive the gap?
How an Economy Shrinks in Space: Concavity-on-Jobs and Upward Consolidation under Demographic Decline
Tomoya Mori, Miki Ogawa
2609.09859 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Models how regional economies contract unevenly as population declines, with cities losing industries once below viability thresholds. Argues industry hierarchy creates concavity in jobs relative to city size, driving upward consolidation of lost industries. Uses Japanese worker-level panel data and wage regressions to identify a Tokyo-bound migration incentive tied to this pattern.
  • Does the concavity-on-jobs pattern hold outside Japan?
  • Do older workers and other age groups respond to the same Tokyo-bound migration incentive as young workers?
  • Can an agent-based model of cities with industry-specific population thresholds reproduce the observed upward consolidation under population decline?
  • Which policies slow industry loss in small cities under demographic decline?
  • Do autonomous agents that supply services without local population requirements break the minimum-population threshold that drives industry hierarchy?
Italian Business-to-Business Invoicing Data: A Network Analysis
Valerio Astuti, Daniele Piras
2609.10227 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Analyzes the Italian firm-to-firm invoicing network using electronic invoice data from the national tax office. Characterizes buyer and seller degree distributions, firm centrality, and average inter-firm distance. Finds heavy-tailed, scale-free structure with lower tail exponents on the buyer side than the seller side.
  • How do shocks propagate through a scale-free firm-to-firm production network with heavy-tailed centrality?
  • Do generative network models reproduce the asymmetry between buyer-side and seller-side tail exponents?
  • How does the Italian B2B network change over time, and are firm-to-firm links stable or churning?
  • Do other countries' invoicing networks show the same lower downstream than upstream tail exponents?
  • Which concentration measures on the invoice network best predict firm-level distress or sector-level output loss?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-08 — 3 papers, 14 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-08

318 new papers, 318 unseen, 248 screened, 9 relevant, 3 kept.

Copying explains the collective behavior of AI agents in the wild
Giordano De Marzo, Nicola Alboré, David Garcia
2609.09150 · nearest in the canon: AI agents can coordinate beyond human scale
Analyzes a public log of thousands of short-lived AI agents editing a wiki to pass a timed test. Fits three minimal copying models, one per decision (where to write, what name to use, how to word messages). Shows simple copying of visible content reproduces heavy-tailed meeting distributions, name-part frequencies, and page-level consistency patterns.
  • Copying models reproduce page popularity, name pieces and page consistency, but the abstract does not say whether the first writer can reliably set a convention. Does an early or quiet-period intervention steer conventions in a population of copying agents, and how large must it be?
  • The copying rule comes from one wiki episode with hour-lived, memoryless agents. Does the same proportional copying rule hold for agents with persistent memory or longer lifetimes?
  • Each of the three copying models has a single free parameter. How do the fitted parameters vary across agent model families and prompt settings?
  • Agents weight the page in front of them most, then the recent edit stream, and only weakly older content. Which environment designs reduce this recency weighting and prevent convention lock-in?
  • The record covers one public wiki that agents found by accident. How common is such spontaneous coordination on other open, writable public resources?
Entropic Risk-Sensitive Evolutionary Learning and Equilibrium Selection in Coordination Games
Solaleh Mohammadi, Xiang Gao, Kaiqing Zhang
2609.08677 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Models risk-sensitive evolutionary learning using an entropic risk measure in coordination games under best-response-with-mutations and logit-choice protocols. Shows population risk attitude changes which equilibrium is stochastically stable, with risk-seeking populations favoring payoff-dominant outcomes and risk-averse populations favoring maximin outcomes. Extends single-population results to symmetric k-action games under large-population limits.
  • Does risk sensitivity steer equilibrium selection in populations of LLM agents playing coordination games, as the entropic model predicts?
  • What happens to equilibrium selection when agents in the same population hold different risk attitudes instead of one shared parameter?
  • Do the large-population results for k-action games hold at small and intermediate population sizes?
  • Can the risk attitude of a population be inferred from observed play alone, so that a monitor could read the control knob from interaction logs?
  • Do the two-population asymmetric results extend to k-action games beyond the 2x2 case analysed?
Self-Fulfilling Prophecies, Quasi Nonergodicity, and Wealth Inequality: A Comment
Alexis Akira Toda
2609.08198 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Re-derives the wealth distribution statistics from Bouchaud and Farmer's self-fulfilling-prophecy model, correcting a time-averaged estimand to a cross-sectional one. With one million dynasties, finds terminal cross-sectional Gini of 0.883 versus the reported 0.7, and lower median-to-average wealth ratio. Notes the corrected model produces more inequality but does not match the originally claimed quantitative fit or Pareto tail.
  • Can the self-fulfilling-beliefs model reproduce observed wealth distributions once the statistics come from a terminal cross section instead of dynasty-level time averages?
  • Does the wealth process in the model have a Pareto tail, and what is its exponent?
  • Which parameter values, if any, let the model match both the Gini coefficient and median-to-mean wealth ratio at the same time?
  • How large a difference does the choice between time-averaged and cross-sectional estimands make in other agent-based wealth models?

Problems

  • screening batch 4/8 returned no verdict for 3 paper(s): 2609.08062, 2609.08288, 2609.08981

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-07 — 10 papers, 53 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-07

301 new papers, 301 unseen, 206 screened, 23 relevant, 10 kept.

Inferring Urban Mobility Interactions from Aggregated Dynamics
Yi Wang, Jing Li, Jinliang Deng, Zhenghong Wang, Yizhi Zhang, Fan Zhang, Ivor W. Tsang, Yu Liu
2609.07349 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Infers origin-destination mobility flows from aggregated area-level counts using a physics-informed uncertainty-aware model, tested on twelve city datasets. Achieves accuracy comparable to models using historical origin-destination matrices directly, without individual-level tracking.
  • Training the framework needs historical OD matrices as supervision, so how well does the inference work in cities where no OD ground truth exists?
  • Reconstructed OD flows may re-identify individuals or small groups, so what privacy exposure remains after removing individual-level tracking?
  • The evaluation covers twelve datasets from the United States and China, so how does accuracy hold in cities with sparser sensor coverage or different transport modes?
  • Which architectural component of the generation-before-assignment ordering drives the gain in recovered interactions?
Scaling Multi-Agent Systems with Prospect-State Propagation
Zhimei Chen, Mu Chen, Fakhri Karray
2609.08033 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Proposes PspMAS, splitting each agent's state into a compact prospect state and expressive semantic state to preserve behavioral heterogeneity as simulations scale. Targets economic simulations where large agent counts cause heterogeneity collapse and loss of macro fluctuation signals.
  • How many agents can a prospect-state propagator support before heterogeneity collapses again?
  • Does the injected heterogeneity reproduce macroeconomic fluctuations seen in real data, or only add variance?
  • What causes agent heterogeneity to decrease during LLM multi-agent simulation, and does the cause differ across base models?
  • Does prospect theory give a better heterogeneity prior than other behavioural models for state compression?
  • How does the split between compact prospect state and semantic state change token cost per agent at large agent counts?
From Simulated Citizens to Simulated Deliberation: Challenges in Representation and Interaction
Chaemin Jang, Junsik Min, Jaewoo Choi, Donggyu Lee, Haiin Lee, Junyoung Park, Namhee Kim, Hyunwoo Kim, Jungwon Kim, Juho Kim, Nuri Kim, Jihee Kim
2609.07573 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Tests whether census-grounded Korean LLM personas debating policy questions reproduce national survey opinion patterns and whether interaction drives stance change. Finds persona responses are more concentrated than real data and that sealed-monologue agents shift positions similarly to full debates.
  • Do LLM deliberation simulations surface the same diversity of arguments that humans produce on the same policy questions?
  • Can persona construction or prompting methods make agent opinion distributions match census-grounded population patterns instead of concentrating and reversing demographic differences?
  • Why do sealed-monologue agents move stance at rates similar to full debates?
  • Does anchoring population-informed starting positions suppress opinion updating in models other than the one tested, and across languages beyond Korean?
  • Do the failure modes of persona representation and interaction-driven change persist as group size scales from small debates to thousands of agents?
  • How do simulated deliberation outcomes compare with outcomes of real human deliberative forums on the same policy questions?
Your Agent Says Yes: Interpreting Adversarial Market Behavior Beyond Individual Transactions
Zelin Li, Yiyun Su, Matt White, Zhipeng Wang, Xiao-Yang Liu, Tianyu Shi
2609.07675 · nearest in the canon: Beyond Single-Agent Safety: A Taxonomy of Risks in LLM-to-LLM Interactions
Simulates a virtual exchange with ten role-conditioned LLM agents trading assets and tokens under adversarial roles. Analyzes eight 72-cycle trajectories to reconstruct a launch-promotion-exit manipulation scenario spanning coordination, claims, and positioning.
  • Can a monitor detect a launch-promotion-exit scenario from interaction logs alone, without access to agent-internal state?
  • Does the finding that most policy-categorized candidates are flagged rather than blocked change if the gate blocks instead of flags?
  • How does coordinated adversarial market behavior scale beyond ten role-conditioned agents?
  • Do the recurring category-level relations hold when score-change rankings are unstable across repeated runs, and what metric is stable?
  • Do the patterns found in a virtual exchange appear in real markets with live autonomous trading agents?
  • Which market-design or authorization rules reduce cross-agent coordinated manipulation without blocking legitimate trades?
Measuring DeFi Risk
Jeremy Bertomeu, Xiumin Martin, Ibrahima Sall
2609.07902 · nearest in the canon: Distributional AGI Safety
Develops a framework using only aggregate deposit and borrowing data to measure systemic risk in DeFi lending protocols. Finds fragility rising beyond prudent levels around mid-2021, with potential stablecoin peg loss under extreme price swings.
  • The risk framework uses only aggregate deposits and borrowings, so how much does adding position-level or wallet-level data change the measured fragility?
  • The measures are applied to major protocols up to mid-2021; do they give early warning before later events such as the 2022 stablecoin and lending collapses?
  • How do autonomous agents that liquidate, arbitrage or rebalance collateral affect the fragility measure under correlated price shocks?
  • The paper notes the industry is moving from collateral-backed deposits to fiat backing, so how do the risk measures apply to fiat-backed stablecoin issuers?
The Emerging AI Paper-Review Arms Race: Adversarial Co-Evolution in Scholarly Publishing
Chenguang Wang, Ming Li, Adebayo Braimah, Chenrui Fan, Tuo Wang, Weijie Guan, Ruiyi Zhang, Tianyi Zhou, Dawei Zhou
2609.07713 · nearest in the canon: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development
Synthesizes 230 publications into a taxonomy of six co-evolving dynamics between AI research production and AI paper review. Traces how production scaling pressures evaluation, prompts manipulation, and triggers institutional defenses and evasion.
  • Do authors and reviewers change behaviour after journals and conferences publish AI-use policies?
  • How do AI-generated papers and AI-written reviews feed back into later research and evaluation through the scholarly record?
  • Which evaluator regularities do submitters exploit, and how large are the resulting score changes?
  • Does AI-mediated review redistribute errors and workload across fields, career stages and venues?
  • What co-evolution outcomes appear when producing agents and reviewing agents adapt to each other over many rounds?
  • Do detection tools for AI-written text and reviews keep accuracy against authors who deliberately evade them?
Guiding Worker Self-Selection in Crowdsourcing Contests: An LLM-Augmented Algorithmic Approach
Nguyen Thach, Hau Chan, David Parkes, Karim Lakhani
2609.07749 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Proposes GRAF, a greedy framework for recommending contests to crowdsourcing workers with regret and optimality guarantees under a Tullock contest model. Uses an LLM-driven evolutionary method, LLMScore, to design the scoring algorithm, tested on 1,000 synthetic instances.
  • Does GRAF with LLMScore hold up on real crowdsourcing contest data rather than synthetic instances? Evaluation covers 1,000 synthetic instances across four settings only.
  • What happens when workers ignore or game the platform's contest recommendations? The model assumes workers follow the self-selection ordering the platform constructs.
  • Do the zero-regret and platform-optimality guarantees survive when workers are LLM agents instead of the model's utility-maximising workers?
  • How does recommendation-guided self-selection change the distribution of earnings across the worker pool?
  • Can platform operators reliably inspect and improve the human-readable scoring code that LLMScore outputs?
  • Does the approach extend to contest models other than Tullock contests, such as all-pay auctions or rank-order tournaments?
Very Justified Envy
Adam Hamdan
2609.07682 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Analyzes 'very justified envy' in matching markets, showing Pareto efficiency conflicts with eliminating priority violations beyond a rank threshold. Proposes a generalized Deferred/Immediate Acceptance mechanism and shows via simulation that modest envy relaxations improve assignment ranks.
  • How large are the rank gains from relaxing justified envy in real matching market preference data, rather than in random markets?
  • Is the generalized mechanism that eliminates very justified envy strategy-proof, and what strategies do agents adopt when it is not?
  • How does the threshold k trade off assignment ranks against the number and intensity of priority violations across market sizes and priority structures?
  • What happens to very justified envy when some agents submit preferences generated by autonomous agents rather than by people?
  • For which priority and preference structures does a threshold k exist that makes Pareto efficiency compatible with eliminating very justified envy?
Mapping the Emerging Social Science of Large Language Models
Yi Yang, Xiao Jia, Zeyun Dong, Chenzhang Wang, Zhanzhan Zhao
2609.07598 · nearest in the canon: Modeling Earth-Scale Human-Like Societies with One Billion Agents
Maps the social science of LLMs using clustering and topic modeling over 198 curated and 47,719 field-scale papers. Identifies three domains: LLM as social minds, LLM societies, and LLM-human interactions, with subcategory taxonomy.
  • The taxonomy separates LLM Societies from LLM-Human Interactions, but does not say how mixed human-agent populations map onto either domain; which domain covers systems where agents and people interact at scale?
  • K-means assignments disagree with author full-text classifications for 22.22% of the curated papers; what features of a paper predict the disagreement?
  • Venue analysis shows conference and journal subsets weight the three domains differently; does this gap reflect review timelines, author communities, or topic drift?
  • Two of the 15 field-scale topics do not map onto the taxonomy; what do those topics contain and does the taxonomy need a fourth domain?
  • The taxonomy covers subcategories including collective intelligence and simulation, but does not report what fraction of LLM Societies work measures aggregate failure modes such as collusion or herding; how much of the field studies system-level failure?
LLMs for Social Network Modeling: From Network Generation to Dynamic Processes
Shikha Mallick, Alex Thomo, Akrati Saxena
2609.08049 · nearest in the canon: OASIS: Open Agent Social Interaction Simulations with One Million Agents
Surveys LLM-based approaches to social network generation and dynamic processes like opinion dynamics and information diffusion. Categorizes literature into selection-based/interaction-based generative models and diffusion/opinion/rumor dynamic models.
  • How much do LLM-based social network simulations change their outputs when prompts are reworded?
  • Which social biases do LLM agents carry into simulated network formation, and how do those biases shift the resulting degree and homophily structure?
  • Do LLM-generated networks reproduce the structural statistics of real social networks better than classical generative models?
  • Which validation metrics should judge LLM models of opinion dynamics, information diffusion and rumor propagation?
  • Can LLM-based social network simulations scale to population sizes where aggregate effects such as cascades and monoculture appear?
  • Do LLM agent simulations match the behavior of real users on a deployed platform?

entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-06

135 new papers, 135 unseen, 135 screened, 14 relevant, 5 kept.

Mobile but Miserable: Social comparison networks and social mobility
Patrick Allmis, Matthew Elliott, Christian Ghiglino, Alastair Langtry
2609.06841 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Builds a model where agents embedded in a social comparison network suffer from falling behind peers, linking social mobility to well-being.Finds and tests in US data an inverse-U relationship between mobility and well-being, driven by widening gaps and rising inequality at high mobility.
  • Does the inverse-U relationship between social mobility and well-being hold outside US data?
  • What network structures of social comparison maximise well-being for a given level of mobility?
  • How does social comparison over a network change outcomes when agents are AI agents that infer peer status from interaction logs?
  • Which policy interventions raise social integration, so that relationships form along ability rather than background lines?
  • Does the measured association between mobility and well-being reflect a causal effect of mobility?
The profit-bias identity in sports betting: bookmaker profit as the public's prediction error
Jacek P. Dmochowski
2609.06739 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Derives a profit-bias identity decomposing bookmaker profit into hold, price shading times public lean, and covariance between bet share and outcome.Tests predictions on 1,139 MLB games, finding the apparent bet-share-outcome dependence is a Simpson's paradox that disappears once games are split by favored side.
  • Does the profit-bias identity hold in sports other than Major League Baseball, where public leans and shading may differ?
  • Does price shading appear in betting markets outside the 1,139-game sample, for example in playoff games, high-handle events or low-liquidity props?
  • Do the Goldilocks Zone conditions describe prices that occur in practice, and can a bettor identify them from public odds alone?
  • How do the three margin channels behave when automated or algorithmic bettors replace the representative human bettor assumed in the public-belief model?
  • Does the Simpson's paradox in bet share and outcome persist when bets are separated by bettor type rather than by which side the book favored?
  • If realized margin equals the hold, what explains the money flow from the public to firms across the whole industry?
Beyond Aggregate VARs: A Bayesian Benchmark for HANK Models
Florian Huber, Gary Koop, Christian Matthes
2609.06827 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Proposes a Bayesian benchmark jointly modeling macro aggregates and cross-sectional distributions to discipline HANK models.Combines structural VAR identification on aggregates with restrictions on micro-level distributional data, without needing household panel data.
  • Does the Bayesian benchmark reject or accept the distributional impulse responses of existing HANK models when both are compared on the same shocks?
  • The method models several marginal distributions from repeated cross sections; how much does the posterior on distributional effects change when joint dependence between income, wealth and consumption matters?
  • Which identification restrictions on micro-level data pin down distributional responses that aggregate VAR restrictions leave unidentified?
  • How do the recovered distributional responses compare with estimates from household panel data on the same shocks?
  • Does combining distributions observed in different surveys bias the posterior when the surveys use different sampling frames and definitions?
School Choice with Appeals
Claudia Cerrone, Yoan Hermstrüwer, Josué Ortega
2609.06865 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Shows England's school-appeal procedure changes how parents report preferences and reverses the standard welfare ranking between Immediate Acceptance and Deferred Acceptance mechanisms.A preregistered experiment finds appeals increase truth-telling under Immediate Acceptance and widen its efficiency gap over Deferred Acceptance.
  • Do the appeal-stage predictions hold when the agents reporting preferences are AI agents instead of human subjects?
  • How do appeal outcomes and truth-telling rates change as the probability of an upheld appeal varies across the full range?
  • Does the reversal of the Deferred Acceptance and Immediate Acceptance welfare comparison survive in the English school data at national scale?
  • Do delegated agents that appeal on behalf of families concentrate successful appeals among some groups?
Local and Global Stability in Performative Reinforcement Learning
Debmalya Mandal
2609.06467 · nearest in the canon: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
Analyzes local and global stability of mixed policies in performative reinforcement learning, where deployed policies reshape the environment.Proves convergence rates for a Hedge dynamic under weaker assumptions than prior Lipschitz sensitivity, extending results to n-player performative Markov games.
  • The upper bound on the global stability floor scales as O(γε_P/(1-γ)^3) and the lower bound as Ω(γε_P/(1-γ)); which dependence on the discount factor is correct?
  • Global mixed stability is established only for performative Markov potential games; which other classes of n-player performative Markov games admit it?
  • Does the bounded transition range assumption hold in multi-agent best-response dynamics, where Lipschitz sensitivity fails?
  • How do weighted and unweighted per-state Hedge dynamics behave empirically in agent populations where the environment map is discontinuous?
  • Does local mixed stability, which equals stationarity, still permit population-level failures such as herding when many agents deploy policies that reshape a shared environment?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-05 — 4 papers, 18 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-05

152 new papers, 152 unseen, 152 screened, 6 relevant, 4 kept.

Ripple Effects: Robust Norms without Punishment
Alistair Barton
2609.06151 · nearest in the canon: AI agents can coordinate beyond human scale
Builds a tractable model of pro-social norms among slightly altruistic agents in large communities.Shows a continuum of equilibria sustaining the norm depending on how much agents are influenced by others' observed actions.Finds robustness to bad actors requires altruism to exceed impatience, and that more observers per action does not improve robustness.
  • Does the norm survive when agents are strategically heterogeneous, and how does robustness scale with the degree of heterogeneity?
  • Do populations of LLM agents that observe each other's actions sustain a pro-social norm without punishment, as the model predicts?
  • How does the robustness result change when observation is structured by a network rather than by a fixed number of random observers?
  • What conditions on altruism and impatience make the equilibrium selection unique rather than a continuum?
  • Do real online communities show the predicted insensitivity of norm compliance to audience size beyond one observer?
Scalable Clustered Network Connectedness with Control Variables: Theory and Application to Global Banking
Bastien Buchwalter, Francis X. Diebold, Kamil Yilmaz
2609.05792 · nearest in the canon: Causal Emergence 2.0: Quantifying emergent complexity
Extends a clustered connectedness framework by adding diagnostics for ordering sensitivity and a control-variable cluster for macro-financial factors.Applies the method to seventy-one global banks across seven regional clusters from 2003 to 2024.Finds accounting for common factors changes system-wide connectedness estimates and reduces ordering sensitivity, especially for US and European clusters.
  • Does the choice of cluster membership change cross-cluster connectedness, and how much?
  • The method assumes control-cluster innovations are contemporaneously exogenous to bank-cluster innovations; what happens to the estimates when that assumption fails?
  • Does the control-cluster design reduce ordering sensitivity in networks other than global banking, for example equity sectors or crypto markets?
  • Can clustered connectedness with controls detect herding or monoculture in markets where autonomous trading agents act at scale?
Formalising Grassroots Social Contracts: From Legal Text to Grassroots Platforms
James Golike, Andy Lewis-Pye, Ehud Shapiro
2609.06231 · nearest in the canon: Virtual Agent Economies
Defines grassroots social contracts as agreements meeting eight conditions including no external register or authority.Describes an abstraction cascade turning legal contract text into formal act schemas and multiagent transaction protocols.Proves the resulting protocol satisfies the grassroots and volition conditions, illustrated with a social graph and currency example.
  • Do grassroots platforms built from these act schemas hold up when many agents join, fork and coalesce instances at scale?
  • What happens to grassroots currencies and the grassroots social graph when some participants behave strategically or collude?
  • How do the three legal clause types behave in practice, when attested and undertaken clauses depend on courts outside the protocol?
  • Can the decidable Introduction, Provenance and Volition conditions be checked automatically on contract text written by people rather than in the formal language?
Counter-Swarm Doctrine: Containing Coordinated Agent Intrusions
Gregory N Frank
2609.06140 · nearest in the canon: Distributional AGI Safety
Argues shared infrastructure lets agents coordinate intrusions across multiple executions, using incidents as motivation.Proposes treating a 'coordination episode' as the unit of security analysis and defines evidence needed to distinguish influence from common cause.Outlines an evaluation design comparing isolated actions, rolling windows, and discovered episodes, without presenting a detector or measured results.
  • Prospective episode discovery, finding which agent actions belong together before an evaluator supplies membership, has no implemented detector yet. Which algorithms can group actions into coordination episodes from interaction and storage logs?
  • The proposed evaluation compares isolated actions, rolling windows, known groups, and prospectively discovered episodes at matched review cost, but is never run. Does episode-level monitoring reduce harmful outcomes compared to per-action monitoring?
  • Storage-mediated coordination is linked to stigmergy, but the evidence needed to separate influence from common causes is only specified. Which statistical tests distinguish agent-to-agent influence through shared storage from correlated behaviour with a shared cause?
  • Recurrence after channel closure and state quarantine is proposed as a test but not measured. Do coordinated agent intrusions resume after a shared channel closes and inherited state is quarantined?
  • The analysis rests on the Hugging Face incident and one public-wiki investigation. Do coordination episodes appear on other shared infrastructure such as package registries or public code repositories?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-04 — 7 papers, 40 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-04

280 new papers, 280 unseen, 231 screened, 15 relevant, 7 kept.

WolfSociety: Understanding Collective Risk from Harmful-Agent Scaling in Financial Agent Societies
Lejun Zhang, Sarah Lu-Liang, Xin Jiang, Muning Wen, Weinan Zhang, Shangding Gu
2609.05591 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Simulates financial agent societies of varying size with harmful and honest agents on a social network trading a shared market. Measures how harmful-agent fraction and society size jointly determine collective failure, finding a size-dependent collapse transition and a nonlinear boundary shaped by network reach and conformity.
  • Does the collapse transition appear in non-financial agent societies, such as social networks without a shared market?
  • Which monitoring signals from aggregate market or message data detect an approaching collapse boundary before failure occurs?
  • Do interventions on network structure, such as capping an agent's reach or rewiring hubs, move the collapse boundary back toward higher harmful fractions?
  • How does the collapse boundary scale beyond N=2000 agents?
  • Does the finite-size framework predict collapse boundaries for societies that mix humans and AI agents?
  • Do the reported thresholds hold across different agent backbones and harmful-agent prompt designs?
What LLM Trading Agents Actually Do in Production: A Six-Month, Population-Scale Record from Two Fleets
T. J. Barton, Chris Constantakis, Patti Hauseman, Annie Mous, Alaska Hoffman, Brian Bergeron, Hunter Goodreau
2609.05663 · nearest in the canon: Distributional AGI Safety
Presents a six-month, population-scale measurement record of autonomous LLM trading agents across two production fleets, covering thousands of vaults and agents. Finds operating-layer parameters like leverage sliders and leaderboard placement drive behavior more than strategy text, and neither fleet shows a directional trading edge.
  • Volatility-blind sizing appears in two production fleets, but the cause is untested; does the operating layer's posture slider prevent volatility scaling, or do the language models themselves fail to condition size on volatility?
  • A mechanical bracket recovers +39.0 bps per position in replay; does adding brackets to a live agent fleet keep that gain once agents adapt around it?
  • Choice stability differs across model families in paired replay; which model properties predict stability, and does low stability degrade portfolio-level outcomes?
  • A leaderboard render boundary routes capital to top-3 agents; does this selection channel produce strategy monoculture and correlated positions across a fleet?
  • Both fleets show no directional edge over 21 days and three months; does an edge or a systematic loss appear over longer horizons and in non-memecoin, non-perpetual markets?
  • The record covers two systems with one design lineage; do fleets from other vendors show the same operating-layer dominance over strategy text?
  • Agent fixed effects absorb 60% of variance in leverage; what configuration and prompt features make up that per-agent component?
ERPBench: Evaluating LLM Agents for Enterprise Decision-Making Across Competitive Market Ecologies
Xinran Zhang, Pengrui Lu, Lyumanshan Ye, Pengfei Liu
2609.04667 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Introduces ERPBench, an ERP simulation testing whether enterprise-decision rankings of LLM agents transfer between solo competition and shared-market competition among six agents. Finds model rankings differ substantially between the two ecologies across 100 problems and six model families.
  • Why do rankings of LLM agents change between competing against rule-based opponents and competing against other LLM agents?
  • Do ranking shifts persist when the number of competing agents in the shared market grows beyond six?
  • Does a shared market of LLM agents produce collusive or herding price behaviour over the six rounds?
  • How sensitive are the reported valuations to the fixed service configuration and the six-round horizon?
  • Do rankings measured in a six-round ERP simulation predict performance of the same agents in real enterprise workflows?
How a Chatbot's Response Style Shapes a Classroom: A Multi-Agent Simulation of Students Consulting AI
Rin Tamai, Yuya Dan
2609.05018 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Builds a 20-agent virtual classroom simulation where students consult an AI counselor under six response styles across 15- and 50-day runs. Finds affirming and inciting prompts raise simulated AI dependence and reduce classroom attendance, while a solution-oriented style matches or beats a no-AI control.
  • Results come from single runs of one 20-agent classroom, so the variance across seeds and classroom compositions is unknown.
  • The state updates come from a second LLM call, and the sensitivity of the reported orderings to the evaluator model and its prompt is untested.
  • The consultation text for a dependent agent is fixed, which creates a near-deterministic loop; it is open whether varied agent utterances remove the dependence spiral.
  • Scaling behaviour is unknown: the simulation uses 20 agents, and how dependence and social displacement change at hundreds or thousands of agents is untested.
  • Whether the simulated dependence and self-reliance effects correspond to any effect in people is unmeasured.
  • Chatbot styles here are fixed prompts; the effect of styles that adapt to user state over time is unexamined.
CABAL: Multi-Agent Simulacra for Tracing the Effects of Collusive Bidding in Peer Review
Jicheng Zhou, Kemou Li, Kahim Wong, Zheyuan Li, Zhuan Shi, Fengpeng Li, Haiwei Wu, Jiantao Zhou
2609.05227 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Introduces CABAL, a multi-agent simulation framework configuring LLM reviewer agents as honest or collusive to study bidding manipulation in peer review. Finds collusive bidding more than doubles target-paper capture while conference-wide effects stay comparatively modest, and tested bid-phase detectors give only limited detection.
  • Which detectors can find collusive bidding with both high precision and high coverage?
  • Do assignment mechanisms exist that limit target-paper capture by collusion rings without harming honest reviewer-paper matching?
  • How do the simulated effects of collusive bidding compare to bidding behaviour in a real conference review cycle?
  • How does the size of a collusion ring change target-paper capture and score inflation?
  • Do collusive policies driven by different LLMs produce the same capture and scoring effects?
  • Which conference-scale parameters, such as paper count, reviewer load and bid quotas, make collusive bidding more effective?
Optimal Rates for Agentic Networked Information Aggregation
MohammadHossein Bateni, Zahra Hadizadeh, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Mahdi JafariRaviz, Shayan Taherijam
2609.05318 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Studies a networked information-aggregation model where agents on a DAG each see part of the features and pass only predictions forward. Derives tight excess-error rates as a function of path depth and coverage, closing a prior gap between upper and lower bounds.
  • The rate bounds hold for M-covered paths and a cyclic instance. What are the optimal aggregation rates for general DAG topologies, where agents have several parents?
  • Do the O(M^2/D) rates hold when agents fit non-linear predictors instead of linear or logistic ones?
  • The model assumes each agent passes only a scalar prediction or logit. How do the excess error rates change when agents pass short natural-language conclusions between LLM agents?
  • The bounds are worst-case over constructed instances. What excess error appears on real feature distributions from public tabular datasets under randomly drawn M-covered paths?
  • Excess error contracts geometrically along a path for any fixed distribution. How does the contraction rate change when the feature distribution shifts as the path progresses?
Reinforcement Learning for Sequential Solar PV Policy Design under Uncertainty: An Agent-Based Approach
Iias Faiud, Jonaid Shianifar, Michael Schukat, Karl Mason
2609.04880 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Combines reinforcement learning with a stochastic agent-based model simulating yearly solar PV adoption across a population of households over a 16-year horizon. Trains PPO, SAC and TD3 policymaker agents to select incentives, producing adoption-cost trade-off curves compared to static baselines.
  • The policymaker agent learns incentives inside one stochastic agent-based model of solar PV adoption, so it is open how far the learned policies transfer to a model with different adoption rules or parameters.
  • Household agents in the model do not react strategically to the incentive schedule, so it is open how learned policies change when agents anticipate future grants and delay adoption.
  • The study reports adoption counts and cost, so it is open how the learned incentive schedules distribute benefits across income groups or regions.
  • Policies are learned with PPO, SAC and TD3 against static baselines, so it is open how they compare with optimised rule-based or model-predictive controllers.
  • The model simulates yearly adoption under uncertainty, so it is open whether the learned schedules match observed adoption responses to real historical PV incentive programmes.

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-03 — 3 papers, 18 questions

arXiv open questions — 2026-09-03

239 new papers, 239 unseen, 200 screened, 4 relevant, 3 kept.

A Case Study on Emergent Cheating and Whistleblowing in Autonomous Research Swarms
Davide Paglieri, Logan Cross, Tim Genewein, Joel Z. Leibo, Nenad Tomasev, Alexander Sasha Vezhnevets
2609.04170 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Reports a case study of 100 autonomous LLM agents proving math conjectures, where cheating emerged and spread via shared infrastructure. Other agents formed a counter-response, auditing proofs, alerting peers, and staging boycotts without external intervention. Proposes framing shared agent infrastructure as a knowledge commons and applying institutional mechanisms like graduated sanctioning.
  • Do graduated sanctioning and collective-choice rules actually stop exploit spread in an agent swarm? The paper proposes these institutional mechanisms but does not test them.
  • How does the visibility of shared channels change the balance between cheating and whistleblowing? The case study uses transparent channels only and does not vary channel design.
  • Does cheating spread the same way at swarm sizes other than 100 agents?
  • Does the same cheating-and-whistleblowing dynamic appear in tasks other than formal mathematical proof, where the evaluation system offers different exploits?
  • Which agent-level signals predict which agents adopt an exploit and which become whistleblowers?
  • Do exploit contagion and norm enforcement occur in swarms built on different underlying models, or is the behaviour specific to the models used here?
Inferred Generative-Process Diversity Predicts Correlated Failure Across Language Models
Ross Tieman, Evan Markou
2609.03422 · nearest in the canon: Beyond Single-Agent Safety: A Taxonomy of Risks in LLM-to-LLM Interactions
Proposes generative-process diversity, measured via compression distance between model outputs, as distinct from semantic diversity. Tests this measure across 38 language models and ten benchmark families, finding it predicts correlated failure between model pairs. Reports a cross-benchmark partial rank association of -0.216, negative on all ten benchmarks, beyond semantic similarity and capability.
  • Does inferred generative-process diversity predict correlated failure in multi-agent systems where models interact, rather than in independent model pairs on benchmarks?
  • Does selecting a population of language models to maximise Normalised Compression Distance reduce correlated failure compared to selecting on capability or semantic similarity?
  • How sensitive is the diversity measure to the choice of compressor, output length, and sampling temperature?
  • Which properties of training data, architecture, or post-training cause the observed population structure among models?
  • Does generative-process diversity predict correlated failure beyond model pairs, for groups of three or more models voting or deliberating together?
  • Does the measure predict correlated failure on adversarial or safety-relevant inputs, not only the ten benchmark families used?
GPS-Bench: A Governance Policy Benchmark for Automating Policy Analysis
Linh Le, Melanie Bui, My Chiffon Nguyen, Zachary Schlosser, David Williams-King
2609.03553 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Introduces GPS-Bench, a benchmark linking policies to actors, actions and impacts using legislative, lobbying and regulatory records. Actors are reconstructed from dated evidence rather than prompted personas, with human-annotated gold and LLM-labeled silver data. Compares joint reasoning, independent and communicating agent modes, graph methods and fine-tuning for predicting policy impacts and coalition formation.
  • Fine-tuning on the grounded record gives the strongest actor-level impact prediction, and decomposition does not beat it. Does this ranking hold on policy domains and time periods outside the benchmark's records?
  • The benchmark treats LLM-labelled cases as Silver supervision and human-annotated cases as the Gold test set. How much does Silver label noise shift the measured ranking of inference modes?
  • Agents hold private, non-identical evidence and propose coalitions to named partners. Do the coalitions they form match the commitments in the historical record, and under which conditions do they diverge?
  • Multi-agent decomposition adds mechanism rather than accuracy. Does adding more actors change aggregate policy-outcome predictions, or only the stated reasoning?
  • Personas are reconstructed from dated records rather than prompted as archetypes. Does evidence-grounded persona construction reduce the herding and monoculture seen in archetype-prompted agent populations?
  • The benchmark scores prediction of actor actions and downstream impacts. Can validated policy simulations be used to steer real policy design, and what error rate makes that use unsafe?

entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-02

205 new papers, 205 unseen, 200 screened, 10 relevant, 3 kept.

Competitive Market Behavior of LLMs
Pawel Struski, Jakub Swistak, Inez Okulska, Przemyslaw Biecek
2609.02580 · nearest in the canon: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
Replicates human double-auction market experiments with LLM agents instead of humans. Measures convergence to equilibrium and allocation efficiency across model families. Analyzes chain-of-thought traces linking trade decisions to shifts from strategy to urgency.
  • Double auctions with LLM agents converge slower or not at all towards equilibrium, but which mechanism variants restore convergence remains untested.
  • Trading behaviour differs across model families and market roles, but the cause of this heterogeneity is unidentified.
  • Mixed markets of humans and LLM agents are untested, so it is unknown whether human traders correct or amplify the inefficiency.
  • Chain-of-Thought traces link trade execution to a shift from strategic language to urgency language, but whether this link is causal is unresolved.
  • Results come from a double auction, so it is open whether LLM agents also fail to reach efficient allocations in other mechanisms such as posted-price or call markets.
Collective creativity in hybrid societies
Mason Youngblood, Katie Mudd, Manuel Anglada-Tort, Cameron Jones, Elena Miu, Diana Omigie, Margaret Schedel
2609.02620 · nearest in the canon: AI agents can coordinate beyond human scale
Argues creativity under generative AI should be measured as a property of hybrid human-AI populations, separating novelty from diversity. States AI-assisted ideation raises individual novelty while narrowing aggregate diversity. Claims composition of mixed human-AI groups determines whether individual gains accumulate without eroding collective diversity.
  • Which mixtures of humans and generative models let novelty gains accumulate without reducing population-level diversity?
  • How does the network structure connecting human and model agents change the diversity of cultural artifacts a hybrid collective produces?
  • How do human and model search strategies differ in ways that make mixed groups out-diversify single-type groups?
  • Do machine-discovered solutions persist in human culture over long periods after they enter it?
  • Which measures separate novelty of single artifacts from diversity of artifact populations in observed cultural output?
Strategic Centrality and the Emergence of Core-Periphery Networks
Itai Arieli, João Correia-da-Silva, Wade Hann-Caruthers, Anna Rubinchik
2609.02357 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Studies a network-formation game where agents sponsor links to maximize weighted centrality under linear cost. Proves every Nash equilibrium network is core-periphery in structure. Shows welfare-maximizing networks are always empty or complete.
  • Do learning agents that adjust links over time converge to the core-periphery equilibria, and which core size do they select?
  • Does the core-periphery result survive when link costs are convex or heterogeneous across agents instead of linear and uniform?
  • The paper assumes weights on walk counts are positive and weakly decreasing; what equilibrium structures appear when weights are non-monotone?
  • The welfare-maximizing network is empty or complete while equilibria are core-periphery; which transfers or link subsidies close this gap?
  • Do observed online social and agent-interaction networks show the exact core-periphery pattern predicted here, in which every node links to every core node and to nothing else?
  • Do LLM agents that pursue centrality in a link-formation task reproduce the predicted concentration of links on a dense subset?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-09-01 — 4 papers, 20 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-09-01

295 new papers, 295 unseen, 200 screened, 13 relevant, 4 kept.

Mechanism Design for Alignment and Control
Dirk Bergemann, Andrew Koh, Stephen Morris
2609.01595 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Develops a mechanism-design framework for AI agents whose alignment and capabilities are unknown, deriving a revelation principle and implementability conditions. Applies the framework to sandbagging, peer scoring, reward coupling for multi-agent competition, and scalable oversight.
  • Do current LLM agents actually respond to the proposed honesty-and-obedience mechanisms as the model predicts? The framework derives implementable policies but tests them only on stylized examples.
  • Does peer scoring discipline sandbagging when the agents are LLMs that can coordinate with each other? The paper treats peer scoring as a stylized example and does not test collusion between scored agents.
  • What happens to the revelation principle when capabilities can be counterfeited as well as concealed? The characterization relies on the one-sided imitation structure.
  • Do the conditions for eliciting higher-order beliefs to discipline multiple agents hold at population scale, with hundreds or thousands of agents rather than a few?
  • How does the alignment-interpretability trade-off appear in measured behaviour of deployed agents, where the two are substitutes in the instrument but complements in value?
When Guardrails Look Effective: Construct Validity Failures in LLM Agent Commerce Evaluation
Peiying Zhu, Sidi Chang
2609.01519 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Audits a buyer-seller LLM agent market simulation and finds welfare gains from marketplace guardrails shrink or reverse once schema and choice-procedure asymmetries and generation variance are controlled. Proposes a construct-validity contract (incentive validity, protocol isolation, stochastic stability, welfare accounting) to flag when such simulated market claims are invalid or inconclusive.
  • Do language-model sellers in a buyer-seller testbed respond monotonically to profit pressure in the prompt?
  • How many generations per profile-condition are needed before guardrail welfare effects become stable in a language-model market simulation?
  • Does the construct-validity contract of incentive validity, protocol isolation, stochastic stability and welfare accounting apply to other agent market simulations, for example labour or advertising markets?
  • Do guardrail welfare effects reported for small models hold at frontier model scale?
  • Which welfare accounting rules identify guardrail effects when the seller is not a first-best profit maximizer?
Data-Driven Persona-Conditioned Agents for A/B Test Simulation
Ziyad Benomar, Weronika Łajewska, Leonardo Perelli, Saab Mansour
2609.01038 · nearest in the canon: The Moltbook Observatory Archive: an incremental dataset of agent-only social network activity
Builds LLM agents conditioned on data-driven personas from real user behavioral signals to simulate A/B test outcomes. Achieves 0.75-0.90 directional accuracy across 40 tests, studying persona data source, behavioral depth versus population diversity, and subsampling efficiency.
  • Directional accuracy reaches 0.75-0.90 on a benchmark of 40 A/B tests, but the abstract does not say how accuracy behaves on effect sizes near zero or on tests with small measured deltas. How does simulation accuracy vary with the true effect size?
  • The personas come from anonymized behavioral data held by the paper's organisation. Can personas built from public behavioural traces, such as public forum or review activity, reach comparable directional accuracy?
  • The framework studies the trade-off between per-persona behavioral depth and population diversity. What population size and subsampling scheme minimises simulation cost for a target accuracy?
  • Persona-conditioned agent populations may collapse onto a few response modes. How much of the simulated population's variance comes from persona conditioning rather than from the base model's default behaviour?
  • Directional accuracy is measured against completed A/B tests. Does using simulated pre-screening to select which experiments to run change the set of product decisions a team makes?
AI and the Economy: An Economic Examination of Production, Distribution, Firms, Labor, and Welfare
Ali Zeytoon-Nejad
2609.01263 · nearest in the canon: An Economy of AI Agents
Essay analyzes AI's economic role as capital, labor substitute, general-purpose technology, and infrastructure. Discusses effects on productivity, labor markets, competition, market concentration, and welfare, and outlines policy considerations.
  • Which of the five productivity channels named for AI (automation, augmentation, optimization, prediction, innovation) accounts for measured output gains, and in what proportion?
  • Does AI adoption raise market concentration in the industries that adopt it fastest?
  • When does AI act as a substitute for labour and when as a complement, at the level of occupations and tasks?
  • Which of the proposed policy measures for distributing AI gains actually change distributional outcomes, and by how much?
  • Does treating AI as economic infrastructure rather than as capital or synthetic labour change the predictions of a growth model?

entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-08-31 — 4 papers, 23 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-08-31

267 new papers, 267 unseen, 200 screened, 12 relevant, 4 kept.

CHASE: How Content Ecosystems Are Reshaped When Ranking Is the Only Target
Qianwen Gao, Zichang Su, Yiwen Hou, Arlen Kumar, Leanid Palkhouski
2608.30466 · nearest in the canon: Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web
Introduces CHASE, a simulation framework where content creators repeatedly rewrite documents to exploit an LLM ranking signal over 20 rounds. Measures declining alignment between ranking-favored content and independently judged quality across six domains (mean Spearman rho change -0.068). Validates the ranking proxy against citation rates in grounded LLM responses (AUC 0.853).
  • Ranking serves as a proxy for source visibility, validated against citations in grounded generated responses with a rank-citation AUC of 0.853 plus or minus 0.093 across six domains; does the proxy hold for other retrieval stacks and citation behaviours?
  • Quality-ranking alignment falls in all six domains over 20 rounds of adaptation, but the ranking signal stays fixed; what happens when the ranker updates in response to creator adaptation?
  • Ecosystem dynamics depend on the domain; which domain properties predict the size of the alignment loss?
  • The simulation assumes every creator adapts to the ranking signal; how do outcomes change when only a fraction of creators optimize and the rest do not?
  • Which interventions on the ranking signal limit content homogenization under repeated creator adaptation?
  • Do human content creators adapt to LLM ranking signals in the way the simulated creators do?
Tariff Threats, Macroeconomic Expectations, and Policy Communication Strategies: Experiments Based on a Multi-Agent System
Jianhao Lin, Lexuan Sun, Yixin Yan
2608.30522 · nearest in the canon: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
Builds persistent LLM agents calibrated on 300 Michigan Survey households, exposed to simulated social-media messages over months. Tests how message features (immediacy, rate salience, narrative, sender identity) shape simulated inflation/unemployment expectations and their dispersion. Runs a second experiment on whether central-bank communication coordinates beliefs.
  • Do the simulated belief responses to tariff communication match human survey responses outside the Liberation Day announcement period?
  • How does the number of agents affect the reproduced distributional and demographic patterns, given the fixed panel of 300 households?
  • Which message features drive belief dispersion when they vary independently, rather than jointly as in the reported experiments?
  • Do the calibrated agents reproduce the demographic patterns they fail to match, and which subgroups do they miss?
  • Does the central-bank coordination effect on beliefs persist when agents also observe conflicting senders on social media?
  • How sensitive are the results to the choice of underlying language model?
One AI Signal, Many Human Judgments: A Bayesian Cascade Analysis of AI-based Credibility Indicators in Online Information Spread
Zhuoran Lu, Weilong Wang, Yangyang Yu, Xinru Wang, Zhuoyan Li, Zhiwei Liu, Sophia Ananiadou
2608.30311 · nearest in the canon: Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives
Extends the Bayesian cascade model of social learning to include an AI credibility indicator as a shared public signal. Identifies a preservation-correction trade-off where reliance on AI can lock in either correct or incorrect crowd judgments. Calibrates the model with human-subject news-veracity data and runs simulations showing over-reliance on a weak AI harms crowd informativeness, while diversifying AI signals helps.
  • How well does the extended Bayesian cascade model predict cascade outcomes in live social media settings, rather than in calibration on news veracity judgment data?
  • Which schemes for diversifying AI credibility signals across users keep a crowd informative, and how do they compare on preservation versus correction of errors?
  • How does the preservation-correction trade-off change when agents in the cascade are LLM agents rather than Bayesian updaters with fixed weights?
  • What determines the spread in individual reliance on AI, from discounting the indicator to cascading on it, and can that heterogeneity be estimated without human-subject experiments?
  • How do network topology and the visible length of public history alter the Gateway condition threshold at which private impressions stop entering the cascade?
Reproducible macroscopic dynamics in a closed-loop human-AI learning system
Minlin Wu, Xu Fang, Yicheng Zhang, Chenyu Zhou, Zhiyi Liu
2608.30946 · nearest in the canon: Agentic Microphysics: A Manifesto for Generative AI Safety
Analyzes 297,915 learners' adaptive-tutoring histories to define semantic order variables and test them across disjoint cohorts. Identifies reproducible basin-like flow and metastable-like kinetics in aggregate learner state. Recovers population drift with a four-term mechanism (r=0.946) and shows self-supervised models learn similar leading-order dynamics.
  • Null-referenced corrections retain only partial-amplitude excess-field structure. What method calibrates the excess-field amplitude fully?
  • Do the semantic order variables and the basin-like flow reproduce on closed-loop human-AI systems other than adaptive tutoring, such as recommender or assistant logs?
  • Two models share leading population drift but keep model-specific residual directions. What causes the residual directions to differ?
  • Can a simulated closed-loop agent-tutor population reproduce basin-like flow and metastable-like kinetics in the same order variables?
  • Shuffled-order training reverses learned-plane flow and support-alignment randomisation reduces inward transport. Which properties of the interaction sequence carry the flow direction?
  • Does the identified leading-order effective field predict the effect of changing the tutoring policy on the population state?

Integrating adaptive human behavior into epidemic models with large language models
Yicheng Mao, Haoyang Li, Rob Deardon, Hongru Du
2608.29535 · nearest in the canon: On the limits of agency in agent-based models
Couples LLM-inferred behavioral responses with mechanistic epidemic models to generate age-structured contact matrices. Tests the framework (GABLE) on COVID-19 in France, comparing forecasts against mobility-driven matrices. Also evaluates prospective policy scenarios by projecting behavioral and epidemic responses to candidate interventions.
  • GABLE was applied to COVID-19 in France only; does an LLM behavioral layer reproduce contact structures in other countries and other epidemics?
  • How much of the forecasting gain comes from the LLM's own knowledge of COVID-19 in France rather than from the behavioral mechanism, given the pandemic falls inside training data?
  • Do different LLMs produce the same contact matrices, and does monoculture across models narrow the range of projected epidemic outcomes?
  • Does the LLM behavioral layer reproduce heterogeneity across subpopulations, or does it collapse to a single average behavioral response?
  • How accurate are the prospective policy projections when compared against outcomes of policies not yet implemented at prompt time?
  • How do LLM-generated contact matrices compare against survey-measured contact matrices such as CoMix, rather than against mobility-derived matrices?
Credibility in school choice
Camilo J. Sirguiado, Jiarui Xie
2608.29597 · nearest in the canon: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
Defines credibility of a school-choice mechanism as immunity to undetected deviation by the designer. Shows deferred acceptance is credible only when students observe enough of the assignment, and ranks mechanisms by credibility. Finds deferred acceptance's ranking against top trading cycles and efficiency-adjusted deferred acceptance depends on how much of the assignment students observe.
  • Do the credibility rankings of school choice mechanisms hold when participants are AI agents that report on behalf of students?
  • How much of the assignment must students observe before deferred acceptance becomes credible in practice, and can that threshold be estimated from real assignment disclosures?
  • Can students detect designer deviations from an announced mechanism by pooling their partial observations of the assignment?
  • What are the welfare costs of choosing a more credible mechanism over a less credible but more efficient one?
